markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=48$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu<48$ [A1] where $\mu$ is the population mean [2 marks] (b) $\bar x=46.300$ [A1], $s_{n-1}=1.851$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $df=9$ [A1]; $t=-2.904$ [M1]; $p=0.009$ [A1]; reject $H_0$ since $p<0.05$ [R1]; the population is normally distributed [A1] [5 marks] (d) (44.976, 47.624) [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the sample standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ (the unbiased estimate) in the $t$ statistic; for a one-tailed test the $p$-value comes from one tail only.

subtopic: t-test for the mean mass of cereal boxes
statement: A factory is supposed to fill cereal boxes with a mean mass of $500$ g. An inspector weighs nine randomly chosen boxes (in grams) and wishes to test whether the mean differs from $500$ g. The sample values are: 497.5, 502.1, 495.3, 499.8, 496.4, 503.2, 498.1, 494.9, 500.6. (a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses, defining any symbols. [2] (b) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (c) Perform a $t$-test, stating the degrees of freedom, the $p$-value and your conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level. State any assumption. [5] (d) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean mass in grams. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=500$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu\neq500$ [A1] where $\mu$ is the population mean [2 marks] (b) $\bar x=498.656$ [A1], $s_{n-1}=2.952$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $df=8$ [A1]; $t=-1.366$ [M1]; $p=0.209$ [A1]; do not reject $H_0$ since $p>0.05$ [R1]; the population is normally distributed [A1] [5 marks] (d) (496.387, 500.924) [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a two-sided test double the one-tail probability, or compare $|t|$ with the critical value from both tails.

subtopic: Two-sample pooled t-test on exam scores
statement: Two classes sat the same test. A teacher wants to know whether class $A$ scored higher on average than class $B$. The scores are: Class A: 71, 64, 80, 75, 68, 77, 82, 70. Class B: 66, 59, 72, 63, 70, 61, 68, 65, 60. Assume both populations are normally distributed with equal variances. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [2] (b) Find the pooled estimate of the common variance. [2] (c) Carry out a two-sample pooled $t$-test and state the $p$-value. [3] (d) State your conclusion at the $5\%$ level of significance. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu_A>\mu_B$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_p^2=\dfrac{(n_A-1)s_A^2+(n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A+n_B-2}$ [M1] $=28.851$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=3.251$ [A1]; $df=15$ [A1]; $p=0.003$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Reject $H_0$ since $p<0.05$ [R1]; there is sufficient evidence of a difference in the stated direction [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the pooled variance only when the population variances can be assumed equal; the degrees of freedom are $n_A+n_B-2$.

subtopic: Paired t-test for a training programme
statement: Eight runners record their time (in seconds) for 400 m before and after a training programme. The coach tests whether the programme reduces the mean time. Before: 62.4, 60.1, 65.3, 63.8, 59.7, 66.0, 61.5, 64.2. After: 61.0, 59.8, 63.9, 62.1, 60.2, 64.2, 60.3, 62.8. Let $d$ be the (after $-$ before) difference and assume the differences are normally distributed. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [2] (b) Find the mean and standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ of the differences. [2] (c) Perform a paired $t$-test and state the $p$-value. [3] (d) Conclude at the $5\%$ significance level. [2] (e) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean difference. [2]
tips: In a paired test work with the differences; the null hypothesis is that their mean is zero.

subtopic: Poisson test for the rate of customer calls
statement: A help desk receives calls at an average rate of $12$ per hour. After a website improvement the manager wants to test whether the rate has decreased. In a random half hour period, $2$ calls are received. (a) State the hypotheses in terms of the mean number of events. [2] (b) State the distribution of the number of events $X$ over the observation period under $H_0$. [1] (c) Find the $p$-value for the observation of 2 events and state the conclusion at the $5\%$ level. [3] (d) Find the critical region for the test at the $5\%$ level and the actual probability of a Type I error. [3]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\lambda=12$ per hour [A1]; $H_1:\lambda<12$ per hour [A1] [2 marks] (b) $X\sim\text{Po}(6)$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $P(X\leq2)=0.0620$ [M1][A1]; do not reject $H_0$ as $p>0.05$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) Critical region $X\leq1$ [A1][M1]; $P(\text{Type I})=0.0174$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert the rate to the observation period before testing; for a lower-tail test $p=P(X\leq\text{observed})$.

subtopic: Chi-squared goodness of fit for a spinner by hand
statement: A spinner has four equal sectors numbered 1 to 4. It is spun $80$ times and the frequencies of each number are recorded. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Category} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \text{Observed} & 26 & 15 & 18 & 21 \end{array}$$ (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [2] (b) Find the expected frequencies. [2] (c) Calculate the $\chi^2$ test statistic. [3] (d) The critical value of $\chi^2$ at the $5\%$ level for $3$ degrees of freedom is $7.815$. State the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: the data follow the stated distribution [A1]; $H_1$: they do not [A1] [2 marks] (b) Expected $=n\times p$: 20, 20, 20, 20 [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{(26-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(15-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(18-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(21-20)^2}{20}$ [A1] $=3.3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Do not reject $H_0$ since $3.3<7.815$ [A1]; the data are consistent with the distribution [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Under a uniform model every expected frequency is $n/k$; use a table of $O$, $E$ and $(O-E)^2/E$.

subtopic: Testing a fair die without a calculator
statement: A die is rolled $120$ times. The frequencies of the scores $1$ to $6$ are recorded. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Category} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline \text{Observed} & 16 & 25 & 18 & 22 & 14 & 25 \end{array}$$ (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [2] (b) Find the expected frequencies. [2] (c) Calculate the $\chi^2$ test statistic. [3] (d) The critical value of $\chi^2$ at the $5\%$ level for $5$ degrees of freedom is $11.07$. State the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: the data follow the stated distribution [A1]; $H_1$: they do not [A1] [2 marks] (b) Expected $=n\times p$: 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20 [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{(16-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(25-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(18-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(22-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(14-20)^2}{20} + \dfrac{(25-20)^2}{20}$ [A1] $=5.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Do not reject $H_0$ since $5.5<11.07$ [A1]; the data are consistent with the distribution [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The degrees of freedom are the number of categories minus one, because the total is fixed.

subtopic: One-tailed z-test with known standard deviation
statement: A machine fills bags of flour. The mass of a bag is normally distributed with mean $250$ g and known standard deviation $6$ g. After servicing, the operator suspects the mean mass has decreased. A random sample of $36$ bags has mean mass $248.2$ g. (a) State suitable hypotheses. [2] (b) Calculate the test statistic $z$. [2] (c) The critical value of $z$ for a one-tailed test at the $5\%$ level is $-1.645$. State the conclusion. [2] (d) Find the critical region for the sample mean $\bar X$. [2] (e) Explain what a Type I error would mean in this context. [1]
markscheme: (a) $H_0:\mu=250$ [A1]; $H_1:\mu<250$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z=\dfrac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\dfrac{248.2-250}{6/\sqrt{36}}$ [M1] $=-1.80$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Reject $H_0$ since $-1.80<-1.645$ [A1]; there is evidence that the mean has decreased [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\bar X<250-1.645\times\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{36}}$ [M1] $=248.355$ so $\bar X<248.355$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Concluding that the mean has decreased when it has not [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The standard error of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt n$; the critical value for a lower-tail test is negative.

subtopic: Does a Poisson model fit goals per match?
statement: This question investigates whether the number of goals scored in a football match can be modeled by a Poisson distribution. Over 200 matches in a league, the numbers of goals were: 0 goals in 28 matches, 1 in 62, 2 in 52, 3 in 34, 4 in 16 and 5 in 8 (no match had more than 5 goals). (a) Calculate the mean number of goals per match. [2] (b) Assuming a Poisson distribution with mean $1.86$, find the expected frequencies of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 or more goals in 200 matches. [3] (c) Carry out a $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test at the $5\%$ level. State the hypotheses, the degrees of freedom, the test statistic and the $p$-value. [5] (d) State the conclusion, and explain why one degree of freedom is lost because of the mean. [2] (e) Find the unbiased estimate of the variance of the data. Comment on its value relative to the mean. [3] (f) In the next season, 25 matches produce 58 goals. Test at the $5\%$ level whether the mean number of goals per match has increased from $1.86$. State the hypotheses and the $p$-value. [4] (g) Find the critical region for this test and the probability that the true mean is $2.4$ goals per match yet $H_0$ is not rejected (Type II error). [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{0(28)+1(62)+2(52)+3(34)+4(16)+5(8)}{200}$ [M1] $=1.86$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Using $P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ [M1]: 31.13, 57.91, 53.86, 33.39, 15.53, 8.18 [A1][A1] (the last by subtraction from 1) [3 marks] (c) $H_0$: Poisson model fits; $H_1$: it does not [A1]; $\chi^2=0.698$ [A1]; $df=6-1-1=4$ (one parameter estimated) [A1][A1]; $p=0.952$ [A1] [5 marks] (d) Do not reject $H_0$ as $p>0.05$: the Poisson model is not a poor fit [A1]; the mean was estimated from the data [R1] [2 marks] (e) $s_{n-1}^2=1.709$ [M1][A1]; close to the mean $1.86$, which is a property of the Poisson distribution (mean = variance) [R1] [3 marks] (f) $H_0:\lambda=1.86$, $H_1:\lambda>1.86$ per match [A1]; under $H_0$ the total is $\text{Po}(46.5)$ [A1]; $p=P(X\geq58)=0.0572$ [A1]; do not reject $H_0$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) Critical region $X\geq59$ [A1] (Type I probability 0.0432); Type II $=P(X\leq58\mid\text{Po}(60))=0.4314$ [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Estimating a parameter from the data reduces the degrees of freedom by one for each estimated parameter. For a Poisson test over several matches, add the means: the total of 25 matches has mean $25\lambda$.

subtopic: Discrete random variable with an unknown constant
statement: The discrete random variable $X$ has the probability distribution shown. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|}x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & k & 2k & 3k & 4k \end{array}$$ (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X>E(X))$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\sum P(X=x)=1$ [M1]: $(1+2+3+4)k=1$ so $k=0.1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $E(X^2)=10$ [A1]; $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Values above $3$: 4 [M1]; probability $0.4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The probabilities must sum to $1$; use that to find $k$ before computing any expectation.

subtopic: Expectation and variance without a calculator
statement: A discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution given by the table. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|}x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 2k & 3k & 3k & k & k \end{array}$$ (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X>E(X))$. [2]
tips: Compute $E(X^2)$ separately from $[E(X)]^2$ to avoid errors in the variance.

subtopic: Exact binomial probabilities with fractions
statement: A biased spinner lands on red with probability $\dfrac13$ on each independent spin. It is spun five times. (a) State the distribution of $X$, the number of successes in 5 trials. [1] (b) Find $P(X=2)$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [2] (c) Find the probability of at least one success. [2] (d) Write down $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $X\sim B(5,\frac{1}{3})$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\binom{5}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}$ [M1] $=\frac{80}{243}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-P(X=0)=1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{5}$ [M1] $=\frac{211}{243}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(X)=np=\frac{5}{3}$ [A1]; $\operatorname{Var}(X)=npq=\frac{10}{9}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the binomial coefficient, the power of $p$ and the power of $q$ explicitly, then simplify the fraction.

subtopic: Binomial model with exact answers
statement: A fair coin is tossed six times and $X$ is the number of heads. (a) State the distribution of $X$, the number of successes in 6 trials. [1] (b) Find $P(X=2)$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest form. [2] (c) Find the probability of at least one success. [2] (d) Write down $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$. [2]
tips: With $p=\tfrac12$ every outcome with $k$ heads has probability $1/2^6$, so $P(X=k)=\binom6k/64$.

subtopic: Normal distribution using symmetry and a standard z-value
statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu=50$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. (a) Write down $P(X<\mu)$. [1] (b) Given that $P(X>56)=0.1$ and that $P(Z<1.28)=0.9$ where $Z\sim N(0,1)$, find $\sigma$ to 2 decimal places. [3] (c) Find $P(X<44)$. [2] (d) Find $P(44<X<56)$. [2]
tips: Standardize with $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$; the normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so tail probabilities mirror.

subtopic: Linear combinations of independent normal masses
statement: A shipping company packs parcels. The mass of a large box is normally distributed with mean $12.4$ kg and standard deviation $0.8$ kg, and the mass of a crate is normally distributed with mean $9.6$ kg and standard deviation $1.1$ kg. All masses are independent. (a) Find the mean and variance of the total mass $W$ of four boxes and one crate. [3] (b) Find $P(W>64.2)$. [2] (c) Find the probability that a randomly chosen box is heavier than a randomly chosen crate. [3]
tips: The variance of a sum of independent variables is the sum of the variances; for a sum of four boxes use $4\sigma^2$, not $(4\sigma)^2$.

subtopic: Delivery times: normal, binomial and Poisson models
statement: This question investigates the lateness of deliveries. The delivery time $T$ minutes of a courier company is normally distributed with mean $32$ and standard deviation $6$. A delivery is late if it takes more than $45$ minutes. (a) Find the probability $p$ that a delivery is late. Give your answer to 4 decimal places. [2] (b) On a day the courier makes $40$ deliveries. Let $L$ be the number that are late. State the distribution of $L$ and find $P(L\geq3)$. [4] (c) Find the mean and standard deviation of $L$. [2] (d) The company refunds \$8 for each late delivery. Find the expected refund per day, and the probability that more than \$24 is refunded on a day. [3] (e) Find the time $t$ such that $95\%$ of deliveries take less than $t$ minutes. [2] (f) The company wants the probability of a late delivery to be at most $0.02$, by reducing the mean delivery time $\mu$ while the standard deviation stays $6$. Find the greatest allowable mean. [3] (g) Because $p$ is small, $L$ is approximated by a Poisson random variable with mean $40p$. Compare the exact binomial probability $P(L=2)$ with the Poisson approximation. [4] (h) Explain why the variance of the binomial distribution is close to its mean when $p$ is small, and why this supports the Poisson approximation. [2] (i) Over a five-day week there are $200$ deliveries. Find $P(\text{at least }8\text{ late deliveries})$ using both the exact binomial and the Poisson approximation. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(T>45)$ [M1] $=0.0151$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $L\sim B(40,0.0151)$ [A1][A1]; $P(L\geq3)=1-P(L\leq2)$ [M1] $=0.0226$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $E(L)=40p=0.605$ [A1]; $\sigma=\sqrt{40p(1-p)}=0.772$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $E(\text{refund})=8E(L)=\$4.84$ [A1]; refund $>\$24$ means $L\geq4$ [M1]; $P(L\geq4)=0.0031$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P(T<t)=0.95$ [M1] $t=41.9$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (f) $P(T>45)\leq0.02$ so $\dfrac{45-\mu}{6}\geq z_{0.98}$ [M1]; $z_{0.98}=2.0537$ [A1]; $\mu\leq32.68$ [A1] [3 marks] (g) Binomial: $0.1000$ [A1]; Poisson with mean $0.605$: $0.1000$ [A1][M1]; the values are close (difference $0.0001$) [A1] [4 marks] (h) $\operatorname{Var}(L)=np(1-p)\approx np=E(L)$ when $1-p\approx1$ [A1]; a Poisson distribution has equal mean and variance [R1] [2 marks] (i) Binomial: $0.0118$ [A1]; Poisson: $0.0125$ [A1]; the approximation is close for large $n$ and small $p$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A normal probability gives $p$; counting how many of $n$ independent deliveries are late is binomial; when $n$ is large and $p$ small a Poisson model with mean $np$ is a good approximation.

subtopic: Venn diagram probabilities and independence
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=\dfrac25$, $P(B)=\dfrac12$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac15$. (a) Find $P(A\cup B)$. [2] (b) Find the probability that neither event occurs. [1] (c) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (d) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $=0.7$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-0.7=0.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ [M1] $=0.4$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(A)P(B)=0.2$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.2$ [M1]; they are equal so the events are independent [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Independent events satisfy $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$; compare the product with the given intersection.

subtopic: Conditional probability and independence check
statement: For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A)=\dfrac38$, $P(B)=\dfrac13$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac18$. (a) Find $P(A\cup B)$. [2] (b) Find the probability that neither event occurs. [1] (c) Find $P(A\mid B)$. [2] (d) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, justifying your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1] $=\frac{7}{12}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1-\frac{7}{12}=\frac{5}{12}$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ [M1] $=0.375$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(A)P(B)=0.125$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.125$ [M1]; they are equal so the events are independent [A1] [2 marks]
tips: $P(A\mid B)$ divides by $P(B)$, the probability of the given event, not by $P(A)$.

subtopic: Two counters drawn without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red and $3$ blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that both counters are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the counters are different colors. [2] (c) Given that the second counter is red, find the probability that the first counter was also red. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{4}{7}$ [M1] $=\frac{5}{14}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P=1-P(RR)-P(BB)$ [M1] $=\frac{15}{28}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(\text{2nd red})=\dfrac{5}{8}\cdot\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{3}{8}\cdot\dfrac{5}{7}=0.625$ [A1]; conditional $\dfrac{P(RR)}{P(\text{2nd red})}$ [M1] $=\frac{4}{7}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Draw a tree diagram; after the first draw the numbers in the bag change.

subtopic: Interpreting a positive test result
statement: A condition affects $1\%$ of a population. A screening test is positive for $90\%$ of people who have the condition and negative for $95\%$ of people who do not. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen person tests positive. [3] (b) Given a positive test, find the probability the person has the condition. [3] (c) Explain, in context, why this probability is much lower than the test's sensitivity. [1]
markscheme: (a) $P(+)=P(D)P(+\mid D)+P(D')P(+\mid D')$ [M1]$=0.01(0.9)+0.99(0.05)$ [A1] $=0.0585$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{P(D\cap +)}{P(+)}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{0.009}{0.0585}$ [A1] $=\frac{2}{13}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Most positive results come from the large healthy group (false positives), because the condition is rare [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use a tree diagram: the denominator of the conditional probability is the total probability of a positive test.

subtopic: Conditional probability from a two-way table
statement: A survey of 250 commuters classified each by how they travel and whether they arrive late. Frequencies: $\begin{pmatrix} 48 & 62 \\ 32 & 108 \end{pmatrix}$ (rows: bus or train, car; columns: late, on time) (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen person is in the first row. [1] (b) Find the probability that a person is in the first row, given that they are in the first column. [2] (c) Determine whether being in the first row and being in the first column are independent events. [3] (d) Two different people are chosen at random without replacement. Find the probability that both are in the first column. [3]
tips: Conditional probability restricts the sample space to the given group; the denominator is that group's total.

subtopic: Expected winnings in a spinner game
statement: In a game, a player spins a spinner with sectors worth \$0, \$2, \$5 and \$20 with probabilities $\dfrac{9}{20}$, $\dfrac{3}{10}$, $\dfrac15$ and $\dfrac1{20}$ respectively. (a) Find the expected winnings from one play of the game (before the cost to play). [3] (b) The game costs \$3 to play. Find the expected profit per game for the player, and state whether the game is fair. [2] (c) Find the fair price to play, and the number of games after which the organizer expects to make a total profit of \$1000 at the current price. [3]
markscheme: (a) $E=\sum xP(x)$ [M1]: $0(0.45) + 2(0.3) + 5(0.2) + 20(0.05)=2.6$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $2.6-3=-0.4$ [A1]; the game is not fair since the expected profit is not zero [R1] [2 marks] (c) Fair price $=2.6$ [A1]; organizer's profit per game $=0.4$ [M1]; $\dfrac{1000}{0.4}=2500$ games [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A game is fair when the expected profit for the player is zero.

subtopic: Sampling without replacement using combinations
statement: A box contains $20$ components, of which $4$ are defective. An inspector chooses $3$ components at random without replacement. (a) Find the probability that none of the 3 chosen items is defective. [2] (b) Find the probability that exactly one is defective. [2] (c) Find the probability that at least two are defective. [2] (d) Find the expected number of defective items in the sample, and explain why the answer would be the same if sampling were with replacement. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\binom{16}{3}}{\binom{20}{3}}=0.4912$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\binom{4}{1}\binom{16}{2}}{\binom{20}{3}}=0.4211$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-P(0)-P(1)=0.0877$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $E=n\cdot\dfrac{K}{N}=0.60$ [M1][A1]; each item is defective with marginal probability $K/N$, and expectation is additive regardless of dependence [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Counting with combinations avoids tree diagrams: favorable selections divided by all selections.

subtopic: Shared values and the complement rule
statement: Each person in a group has a birthday that is equally likely to be any of $365$ days, independently of others (ignore leap years). A group of $m$ people is chosen. (a) Find the probability that in a group of 5 people at least two share a birthday. [3] (b) Find the smallest group size for which this probability exceeds 0.5. [3]
tips: The complement of 'at least two share' is 'all different', which is a product of decreasing fractions.

subtopic: Conditional probability with binomial and normal models
statement: A phone battery lasts a normally distributed time with mean $48$ hours and standard deviation $9$ hours. A user buys $12$ batteries; each lasts at least $60$ hours independently with the same probability. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen battery lasts at least $60$ hours, to 4 decimal places. [2] (b) Find the probability that a battery lasts more than $45$ hours. [1] (c) Given that a battery lasts more than $45$ hours, find the probability that it lasts less than $60$ hours. [3] (d) Let $N$ be the number of the 12 batteries that last at least $60$ hours. Using the probability from part (a), find $P(N=3)$. [2] (e) Given that at least one battery lasts at least $60$ hours, find the probability that exactly three do. [3]
tips: A conditional probability is a ratio of two probabilities from the same model; evaluate both before dividing.

subtopic: Effect of a linear transformation on mean and standard deviation
statement: On a test marked out of $100$, the $10$ students in a class had mean mark $60$ and standard deviation $8$. (a) Write down the mean and standard deviation of the scores converted using $y=1.5x+10$. [3] (b) A second class has 20 students with mean 64 and standard deviation 8. Find the mean of the combined group of 30 students, if the first class has 10 students with the original mean. [2] (c) Explain why the standard deviation of the combined group cannot be found from the two standard deviations alone. [1]
markscheme: (a) New mean $=1.5(60)+10=100.0$ [M1][A1]; new standard deviation $=1.5\times8=12.0$ (the constant $+10$ does not change the spread) [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{10(60)+20(64)}{30}$ [M1] $=188/3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) The combined variance also depends on how far each group mean is from the overall mean [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Adding a constant shifts the mean but not the spread; multiplying by $a$ multiplies both the mean and the standard deviation by $|a|$.

subtopic: Quartiles and an outlier from twelve values
statement: The ages of twelve people attending a workshop are, in order: 12, 15, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 25, 27, 29, 52 (a) Find the median, the lower quartile and the upper quartile. [3] (b) Find the interquartile range. [1] (c) A value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5\times$IQR below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Show that 52 is an outlier. [3]
tips: With an even number of values split the ordered list into two equal halves; the quartiles are the medians of the halves.

subtopic: Estimating mean and quartiles from grouped data
statement: The table shows the distribution of the lengths of 60 phone calls, in minutes. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Length (min)} & 0\text{--}10 & 10\text{--}20 & 20\text{--}30 & 30\text{--}40 & 40\text{--}50 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 6 & 14 & 25 & 12 & 3 \end{array}$$ (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Estimate the mean, using midpoints of the classes. [2] (c) Estimate the median and the interquartile range using linear interpolation on the cumulative frequency. [4] (d) Use your calculator to find an estimate of the standard deviation. [2]
markscheme: (a) $20$--$30$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 [M1]; $\bar x=23.67$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Cumulative frequencies 6, 20, 45, 57, 60 [M1]; median $\approx24.00$ [A1]; $Q_1\approx16.43$, $Q_3\approx30.00$ [A1]; IQR $\approx13.57$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Enter midpoints and frequencies in the statistics menu [M1]; $\sigma\approx10.08$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Grouped-data estimates treat every value in a class as if it were at the midpoint; the median uses interpolation within the median class.

subtopic: Grouped data for the heights of seedlings
statement: The heights of 60 seedlings after three weeks are summarized. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Height (cm)} & 10\text{--}15 & 15\text{--}20 & 20\text{--}25 & 25\text{--}30 & 30\text{--}35 & 35\text{--}40 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 4 & 9 & 17 & 15 & 10 & 5 \end{array}$$ (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Estimate the mean, using midpoints of the classes. [2] (c) Estimate the median and the interquartile range using linear interpolation on the cumulative frequency. [4] (d) Use your calculator to find an estimate of the standard deviation. [2]
markscheme: (a) $20$--$25$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoints 12.5, 17.5, 22.5, 27.5, 32.5, 37.5 [M1]; $\bar x=25.25$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Cumulative frequencies 4, 13, 30, 45, 55, 60 [M1]; median $\approx25.00$ [A1]; $Q_1\approx20.59$, $Q_3\approx30.00$ [A1]; IQR $\approx9.41$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Enter midpoints and frequencies in the statistics menu [M1]; $\sigma\approx6.67$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the cumulative frequency at the class upper boundary and interpolate between boundaries.

subtopic: Modal class and mean for grouped data
statement: The ages of 50 members of a club are grouped as shown. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Age (years)} & 0\text{--}20 & 20\text{--}40 & 40\text{--}60 & 60\text{--}80 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 8 & 16 & 20 & 6 \end{array}$$ (a) Write down the modal class. [1] (b) Estimate the mean, using midpoints of the classes. [2] (c) Estimate the median and the interquartile range using linear interpolation on the cumulative frequency. [4]
markscheme: (a) $40$--$60$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Midpoints 10, 30, 50, 70 [M1]; $\bar x=39.60$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Cumulative frequencies 8, 24, 44, 50 [M1]; median $\approx41.00$ [A1]; $Q_1\approx25.62$, $Q_3\approx53.50$ [A1]; IQR $\approx27.88$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use class midpoints to estimate the mean; show every product $f\times$ midpoint.

subtopic: Comparing weekly sales at two shops
statement: The weekly sales, in hundreds of units, at two shops were recorded for ten weeks. Shop 1: 34, 41, 38, 45, 50, 36, 42, 39, 44, 95. Shop 2: 48, 52, 47, 55, 50, 49, 53, 51, 46, 54. (a) Use your calculator to find the mean, standard deviation, median and quartiles for each data set. [4] (b) Identify any outliers in each data set using the $1.5\times$IQR rule. [3] (c) Compare the two data sets, referring to both a measure of average and a measure of spread. [3]
markscheme: (a) Shop 1: mean $46.40$, $\sigma=16.79$, median $41.5$, $Q_1=38$, $Q_3=45$ [A2]; Shop 2: mean $50.50$, $\sigma=2.87$, median $50.5$, $Q_1=48$, $Q_3=53$ [A2] [4 marks] (b) Shop 1 fences: (27.50, 55.50), outliers: [95] [M1][A1]; Shop 2 fences: (40.50, 60.50), outliers: none [A1] [3 marks] (c) Shop 2 has the higher median (50.5 against 41.5) [A1]; Shop 2 has the smaller interquartile range (5 against 7), so it is more consistent [A1]; interpretation in context [R1] [3 marks]
tips: An outlier inflates the mean and standard deviation but barely changes the median and IQR.

subtopic: Combining two groups using summary statistics
statement: Two classes sat the same test. Class $X$ has $24$ students with mean score $62.5$ and standard deviation $6.8$. Class $Y$ has $16$ students with mean score $70.2$ and standard deviation $5.4$. (a) Find the mean score of all 40 students. [2] (b) Show that $\sum x^2$ for class $X$ is $24\left(6.8^2+62.5^2\right)$. [2] (c) Find the standard deviation of the combined group of 40 students. [4] (d) Explain why the combined standard deviation is larger than the average of the two individual standard deviations. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{24(62.5)+16(70.2)}{40}$ [M1] $=65.58$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2$ [M1] so $\sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2)$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\sum x^2$ for $X=94859.8$, for $Y=79315.2$ [A1][A1]; combined variance $=\dfrac{174175.0}{40}-65.58^2$ [M1]; $\sigma=7.32$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) The two class means differ, so the combined data are spread about the overall mean as well as within each class [R1][R1] [2 marks]
tips: Recover $\sum x^2$ from $n$, the mean and the variance of each group; then add the totals before computing the combined variance.

subtopic: Spearman's rank correlation by hand
statement: Six students are ranked by their scores in mathematics and physics tests. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Maths score} & 78 & 64 & 91 & 55 & 70 & 83 \\ \hline \text{Physics score} & 72 & 60 & 88 & 61 & 65 & 79 \end{array}$$ (a) Rank each set of values, with rank 1 given to the largest value, and find the difference $d$ in ranks for each pair. [3] (b) Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$. [3] (c) Interpret your value of $r_s$ in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) Ranks of Maths score: 3, 5, 1, 6, 4, 2 [A1]; ranks of Physics score: 3, 6, 1, 5, 4, 2 [A1]; $d$: 0, -1, 0, 1, 0, 0 [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum d^2=2$ [A1]; $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{12}{210}$ [M1] $=\frac{33}{35}\approx0.943$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Strong positive monotonic association [A1]; higher maths score tends to go with higher physics score [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Rank both variables in the same direction, check that the $d$ values sum to zero, and use $r_s=1-6\sum d^2/(n(n^2-1))$.

subtopic: Rank correlation between price and rating
statement: A reviewer compares the price (in dollars) and the rating of eight headphones. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\text{Price} & 120 & 45 & 80 & 200 & 65 & 150 & 95 & 30 \\ \hline \text{Rating} & 7.9 & 6.1 & 8.4 & 9.2 & 5.8 & 7.5 & 6.9 & 4.8 \end{array}$$ (a) Rank each set of values, with rank 1 given to the largest value, and find the difference $d$ in ranks for each pair. [3] (b) Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$. [3] (c) Interpret your value of $r_s$ in context. [2]
markscheme: (a) Ranks of Price: 3, 7, 5, 1, 6, 2, 4, 8 [A1]; ranks of Rating: 3, 6, 2, 1, 7, 4, 5, 8 [A1]; $d$: 0, 1, 3, 0, -1, -2, -1, 0 [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sum d^2=16$ [A1]; $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{96}{504}$ [M1] $=\frac{17}{21}\approx0.810$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Strong positive monotonic association [A1]; higher price tends to go with higher rating [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Ranking the data removes the effect of the actual size of the values, so $r_s$ measures monotonic (not just linear) association.

subtopic: Regression line from summary statistics
statement: For a group of workers the hours of training $x$ and productivity score $y$ have $\bar x=40$, $\bar y=120$, standard deviations $s_x=8$ and $s_y=15$, and correlation coefficient $r=0.8$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Estimate the value of $y$ when $x=50$. [1] (c) Interpret the gradient of the line in context. [2] (d) Explain why using the line to predict $y$ for $x$ far outside the data range is unreliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=0.8\times\dfrac{15}{8}=1.5$ [M1][A1]; line through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-120=1.5(x-40)$ so $y=1.5x+60$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=135$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) For each extra 1 hour of training, the predicted productivity score increases by 1.5 (on average) [A1][R1] [2 marks] (d) The linear relationship may not continue beyond the observed range (extrapolation) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ always passes through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ and has gradient $r s_y/s_x$.

subtopic: Regression of y on x from r and standard deviations
statement: A study of $x$ (average daily temperature, $^\circ$C) and $y$ (heating bill, dollars) gives $\bar x=25$, $\bar y=60$, $s_x=5$, $s_y=12$ and $r=-0.6$. (a) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Estimate the value of $y$ when $x=30$. [1] (c) Interpret the gradient of the line in context. [2] (d) Explain why using the line to predict $y$ for $x$ far outside the data range is unreliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) Gradient $=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=-0.6\times\dfrac{12}{5}=-1.44$ [M1][A1]; line through $(\bar x,\bar y)$: $y-60=-1.44(x-25)$ so $y=-1.44x+96$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=52.8$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) For each extra 1 degree Celsius of temperature, the predicted heating bill in dollars decreases by 1.44 (on average) [A1][R1] [2 marks] (d) The linear relationship may not continue beyond the observed range (extrapolation) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A negative correlation gives a negative gradient: here higher temperatures go with lower heating bills.

subtopic: Linear regression for study time and score
statement: A teacher records the number of hours of revision and the test score of ten students. The data are: hours of revision: 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15; test score: 48, 55, 59, 60, 68, 71, 75, 82, 84, 92. (a) Find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient $r$, and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of test score on hours of revision. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient and the intercept in context. [2] (d) Use the regression line to estimate test score when hours of revision is 11. Comment on the reliability of your estimate. [3] (e) Find the value of hours of revision for which the model predicts test score of 83.3. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.999$ [A1]; strong positive linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=3.348x+41.273$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The gradient $3.348$ is the predicted change in test score per unit increase in hours of revision [A1]; the intercept $41.273$ is the predicted test score when hours of revision is zero (which may not be meaningful) [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=78.11$ [A1]; 11 is inside the range of the data 2--15 [A1]; so the estimate is an interpolation and fairly reliable given the strong correlation [R1] [3 marks] (e) $83.3=3.348x+41.273$ [M1] so $x=12.55$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is used to predict $y$; do not swap the variables.

subtopic: Linear model for temperature and ice cream sales
statement: A vendor records the daily maximum temperature ($^\circ$C) and the number of ice creams sold over eight days. The data are: temperature: 14, 17, 19, 21, 23, 26, 28, 31; ice creams sold: 120, 150, 165, 200, 215, 260, 270, 330. (a) Find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient $r$, and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of ice creams sold on temperature. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient and the intercept in context. [2] (d) Use the regression line to estimate ice creams sold when temperature is 35. Comment on the reliability of your estimate. [3] (e) Find the value of temperature for which the model predicts ice creams sold of 256.5. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.993$ [A1]; strong positive linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=12.070x-56.318$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The gradient $12.070$ is the predicted change in ice creams sold per unit increase in temperature [A1]; the intercept $-56.318$ is the predicted ice creams sold when temperature is zero (which may not be meaningful) [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=366.13$ [A1]; 35 is outside the range of the data 14--31 [A1]; so the estimate is an extrapolation and less reliable [R1] [3 marks] (e) $256.5=12.070x+-56.318$ [M1] so $x=25.92$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Extrapolating beyond the data range assumes the relationship continues, which may not be true.

subtopic: Regression of fuel use against engine size
statement: The engine size (liters) and fuel use (liters per 100 km) are measured for nine cars. The data are: engine size: 1.0, 1.2, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.4, 2.8, 3.0, 3.5; fuel use: 5.1, 5.6, 6.4, 6.9, 7.3, 8.1, 8.8, 9.4, 10.5. (a) Find the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient $r$, and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of fuel use on engine size. [2] (c) Interpret the gradient and the intercept in context. [2] (d) Use the regression line to estimate fuel use when engine size is 2.2. Comment on the reliability of your estimate. [3] (e) Find the value of engine size for which the model predicts fuel use of 9.1. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.999$ [A1]; strong positive linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=2.117x+3.026$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) The gradient $2.117$ is the predicted change in fuel use per unit increase in engine size [A1]; the intercept $3.026$ is the predicted fuel use when engine size is zero (which may not be meaningful) [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=7.68$ [A1]; 2.2 is inside the range of the data 1.0--3.5 [A1]; so the estimate is an interpolation and fairly reliable given the strong correlation [R1] [3 marks] (e) $9.1=2.117x+3.026$ [M1] so $x=2.87$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Check that your calculator is set to regression of $y$ on $x$ and that the list entries are paired correctly.

subtopic: Exponential regression for bacterial growth
statement: A biologist counts the number of bacteria (in thousands) in a culture at hourly intervals. time (hours): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; bacteria count: 2.1, 3.0, 4.4, 6.4, 9.3, 13.5, 19.8. (a) Use exponential regression on your calculator to find the model $y=ab^x$. [2] (b) State the value of $r^2$ obtained on your calculator for the transformed data. Comment on the fit. [2] (c) Interpret the value of $b$ in context. [2] (d) Estimate the bacteria count when time (hours) is 8. [1] (e) Find the time for bacteria count to double according to the model. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=2.081$, $b=1.454$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $r^2=0.9999$ [A1]; close to $1$ so the exponential model is a good fit [R1] [2 marks] (c) Each unit increase in time (hours) multiplies the bacteria count by about $1.454$ [A1], a growth of $45.4\%$ per unit [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=41.7$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $b^t=2$ [M1] gives $t=1.85$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The calculator's exponential regression fits $\ln y$ linearly; $b>1$ means growth.

subtopic: Exponential model for the spread of a post
statement: The number of views (in hundreds) of a video is recorded each day after posting. days: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; views: 1.5, 2.4, 3.9, 6.1, 9.8, 15.4, 24.7. (a) Use exponential regression on your calculator to find the model $y=ab^x$. [2] (b) State the value of $r^2$ obtained on your calculator for the transformed data. Comment on the fit. [2] (c) Interpret the value of $b$ in context. [2] (d) Estimate the views when days is 9. [1] (e) Find the time for views to double according to the model. [2]
markscheme: (a) $a=0.949$, $b=1.593$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $r^2=0.9999$ [A1]; close to $1$ so the exponential model is a good fit [R1] [2 marks] (c) Each unit increase in days multiplies the views by about $1.593$ [A1], a growth of $59.3\%$ per unit [A1] [2 marks] (d) $y=62.8$ [A1] [1 mark] (e) $b^t=2$ [M1] gives $t=1.49$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Interpret $b$ as a growth factor per unit of the explanatory variable.

subtopic: Power model for animal metabolic rate
statement: The body mass (kg) and daily energy use (MJ) of eight mammals are recorded. mass: 0.03, 0.3, 2, 5, 25, 70, 150, 400; energy: 0.12, 0.46, 1.6, 3.0, 9.6, 20.1, 38.0, 82.0. (a) Use power regression on your calculator to find a model of the form $y=ax^b$. [3] (b) Show that taking natural logarithms of both sides gives a linear relationship between $\ln x$ and $\ln y$, and state the gradient and the intercept in terms of $a$ and $b$. [3] (c) Predict energy when mass is 1000. [2] (d) Explain why this type of model suits a quantity that scales as a power of another. [1]
markscheme: (a) $a=1.118$ [A1]; $b=0.690$ [A1]; $y=1.118x^{0.690}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln y=\ln a+b\ln x$ [M1][A1]; gradient $=b$ and intercept $=\ln a$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $y=131.618$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (d) Doubling $x$ multiplies $y$ by the constant factor $2^b$, whatever the starting value [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A straight line on a log-log plot indicates a power law; the gradient on that plot is the exponent $b$.

subtopic: Power law regression and Kepler's third law
statement: This question investigates the relationship between the orbital period $P$ (in Earth years) and the mean distance $a$ from the Sun (in astronomical units, AU) of six planets. Mercury: $a=0.387$, $P=0.241$. Venus: $a=0.723$, $P=0.615$. Earth: $a=1.000$, $P=1.000$. Mars: $a=1.524$, $P=1.881$. Jupiter: $a=5.203$, $P=11.862$. Saturn: $a=9.537$, $P=29.457$. (a) Find the linear regression line of $P$ on $a$ and the correlation coefficient $r$. [3] (b) Explain why a straight line is not an appropriate model, by referring to the data for the inner planets. [2] (c) Use power regression to fit a model $P=ka^b$. Give $k$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Show that taking logarithms gives $\ln P=\ln k+b\ln a$. Find the correlation coefficient between $\ln a$ and $\ln P$. [3] (e) Kepler's third law states that $P^2$ is proportional to $a^3$. Show that this implies $b=\dfrac32$, and compare with your value. [3] (f) Uranus has $a=19.19$ AU. Estimate its period using the power model and using the linear model, and given that the true period is about $84.0$ years, find the percentage error of each estimate. [4] (g) The linear model was fitted to data with $a\leq9.5$. State why this is a limitation for the Uranus estimate. [1] (h) Using $b=1.5$ exactly, find the mean distance from the Sun of a body with an orbital period of $50$ years, in AU to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P=3.180a-2.228$ [A1][A1]; $r=0.9924$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) The line predicts $P=-1.00$ for Mercury, whereas the actual value is $0.241$ [A1]; the data curve upward, so the relationship is not linear [R1] [2 marks] (c) $k=1.000$ [A1], $b=1.500$ [A1]; model $P=1.000a^{1.500}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Take $\ln$ of both sides and use laws of logs [M1][A1]; $r=1.000000$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $P^2=ca^3$ gives $P=\sqrt c\,a^{3/2}$ [M1][A1]; so $b=1.5$, and the fitted value $1.500$ is very close [R1] [3 marks] (f) Power: $84.0$ years [A1], error $0.0\%$ [A1]; linear: $58.8$ years [A1], error $30.0\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) Uranus lies outside the data range, so using the linear model is extrapolation [R1] [1 mark] (h) $50=a^{1.5}$ (with $k=1$) [M1]; $a=50^{2/3}$ [A1]; $a=13.57$ AU [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A straight line on a log-log graph indicates a power law $y=kx^b$, and its gradient is the exponent. Compare model predictions with data outside the fitting range to judge extrapolation.

subtopic: Confidence interval for a mean with known standard deviation
statement: The lengths of bolts produced by a machine are normally distributed with known standard deviation $0.8$ mm. A random sample of $64$ bolts has mean length $50.4$ mm. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. [1] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean, given that the appropriate $z$-value is $1.96$. [3] (c) Write down the width of the interval. [1] (d) The width is to be halved using a larger sample. Show that the sample size must be multiplied by $4$, and state the new sample size. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=\dfrac{0.8}{\sqrt{64}}=0.1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\bar x\pm z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=50.4\pm1.96\times0.1$ [M1][A1]; $(50.204,\,50.596)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\times0.196=0.392$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Width $\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ [R1]; halving the width needs $\sqrt{n}$ doubled, i.e. $n\to4n$ [M1]; new size $256$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The half-width (margin of error) is $z\sigma/\sqrt n$; quadrupling $n$ halves it.

subtopic: A 95% interval for a mean and what happens when n is changed
statement: The time taken for a delivery is normally distributed with standard deviation $9$ minutes. A sample of $81$ deliveries has mean time $36.5$ minutes. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. [1] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean, given that the appropriate $z$-value is $1.96$. [3] (c) Write down the width of the interval. [1] (d) The width is to be halved using a larger sample. Show that the sample size must be multiplied by $4$, and state the new sample size. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{81}}=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\bar x\pm z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=36.5\pm1.96\times1$ [M1][A1]; $(34.54,\,38.46)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\times1.96=3.92$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Width $\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ [R1]; halving the width needs $\sqrt{n}$ doubled, i.e. $n\to4n$ [M1]; new size $324$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Always give the interval in the form $(a,b)$ with $a<b$, and state units.

subtopic: Recovering the mean and standard deviation from an interval
statement: A $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean mass, in grams, of a type of apple is $(47.2,52.8)$. The masses are normally distributed and the interval was found from a sample of $49$ apples using the known population standard deviation. (a) Find the sample mean. [1] (b) Find the margin of error, and hence the standard error $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ of the sample mean (use $z=1.96$). [3] (c) Find the population standard deviation $\sigma$, given that the sample size is 49. [1] (d) Hence find a $90\%$ confidence interval from the same data, given $z=1.645$ for $90\%$. [3] (e) State and explain whether the $90\%$ interval is wider or narrower than the $95\%$ interval. [1]
markscheme: (a) Midpoint of the interval $=\dfrac{47.2+52.8}{2}=50$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) Half-width $=\dfrac{52.8-47.2}{2}=2.8$ [A1]; $1.96\times SE=2.8$ [M1]; $SE=1.429$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sigma=SE\times\sqrt{49}=10$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $z\times SE=1.645\times1.429=2.35$ [M1][A1]; $(47.65,\,52.35)$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Narrower: a smaller $z$ gives a smaller margin of error [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The mean is the midpoint of the interval, and the half-width is the margin of error.

subtopic: Sample size for a given margin of error
statement: The standard deviation of the heights of a certain tree species is known to be $15$ cm. A forester wants to estimate the mean height with a $95\%$ confidence interval of margin of error at most $2$ cm. (a) Write down an inequality for $n$ so that the margin of error of a $95\%$ confidence interval is at most $2$. Use $z=1.96$. [2] (b) Solve the inequality, and state the least sample size. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1.96\times\dfrac{15}{\sqrt n}\leq2$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\sqrt n\geq\dfrac{1.96\times15}{2}=14.7$ [M1]; $n\geq216.09$ [A1]; $n=217$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Round the sample size up, never down, because a sample size must be an integer large enough to meet the requirement.

subtopic: t-interval for the mean lifetime of bulbs
statement: A sample of nine LED bulbs is tested and their lifetimes (in thousands of hours) are recorded. The values are: 24.1, 25.3, 23.8, 26.2, 24.9, 25.7, 23.5, 24.4, 25.0. Assume the population is normally distributed. (a) Calculate the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean. [3] (c) Find a $99\%$ confidence interval. State how it compares with the $95\%$ interval, and why. [3] (d) A claim states that the true mean is 25 thousand hours. Use your $95\%$ interval to comment on this claim. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=24.767$, $s_{n-1}=0.894$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $df=8$ so use the $t$-distribution [R1]; $(24.079,\,25.454)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(23.766,\,25.767)$ [A1]; it is wider [A1] because greater confidence requires a larger critical value [R1] [3 marks] (d) 25 lies inside the interval [A1]; so the claim is consistent with the data [R1] [2 marks]
tips: With an unknown population standard deviation and a small sample, use the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

subtopic: Confidence interval for mean commute time
statement: The commute times (in minutes) of twelve randomly chosen employees are recorded. The values are: 32, 28, 41, 35, 30, 38, 27, 44, 33, 36, 29, 40. Assume the population is normally distributed. (a) Calculate the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation. [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean. [3] (c) Find a $99\%$ confidence interval. State how it compares with the $95\%$ interval, and why. [3] (d) A claim states that the true mean is 30 minutes. Use your $95\%$ interval to comment on this claim. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=34.417$, $s_{n-1}=5.518$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $df=11$ so use the $t$-distribution [R1]; $(30.911,\,37.923)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(29.470,\,39.364)$ [A1]; it is wider [A1] because greater confidence requires a larger critical value [R1] [3 marks] (d) 30 lies outside the interval [A1]; so the claim is not supported at the 5% level [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The calculator's $t$-interval function needs the sample mean, $s_{n-1}$ and $n$, or the raw list.

subtopic: Effect of confidence level and sample size on an interval
statement: The population standard deviation of the volumes of juice in a bottling plant is known to be $4.5$ mL. A sample of $50$ bottles has mean volume $498.6$ mL. (a) Use your calculator to find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean. [2] (b) Find $90\%$ and $99\%$ confidence intervals, and comment on how the width changes with the confidence level. [4] (c) Find the smallest sample size needed for the width of a $95\%$ interval to be at most $0.8$ times its current width. [3] (d) Explain why increasing the sample size reduces the width of a confidence interval. [1]
markscheme: (a) $z$-interval with $\sigma=4.5$, $\bar x=498.6$, $n=50$ [M1]: $(497.353,\,499.847)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) 90%: $(497.553,\,499.647)$ [A1]; 99%: $(496.961,\,500.239)$ [A1]; widths $2.094$, $3.278$ [A1]; higher confidence gives a wider interval [R1] [4 marks] (c) Width $=2\times1.96\times\dfrac{4.5}{\sqrt n}\leq1.996$ [M1][A1]; $n=79$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) The standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ decreases as $n$ increases [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A higher confidence level uses a larger $z$-value, so it gives a wider interval; a larger $n$ narrows it.

subtopic: A confidence interval and a two-sided test
statement: The daily rainfall (mm) in a town on eight randomly chosen days is: 5.2, 5.8, 6.1, 5.5, 6.4, 5.9, 6.2, 5.7. Assume normality. A meteorologist claims the mean daily rainfall is $5.5$ mm. (a) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean. [3] (b) State whether the claim is consistent with your interval. [1] (c) Carry out a two-sided $t$-test of $H_0:\mu=5.5$ at the $5\%$ level and state the $p$-value. [3] (d) Explain how the result of the test relates to your confidence interval. [2] (e) Find a $90\%$ confidence interval and comment on whether $5.5$ lies inside it. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=5.850$, $s_{n-1}=0.389$ [A1]; $(5.525,\,6.175)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $5.5$ lies outside the interval [A1] [1 mark] (c) $t=2.544$, $df=7$ [A1]; $p=0.0384$ [A1]; reject $H_0$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) A two-sided test at the $5\%$ level rejects $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ exactly when $\mu_0$ lies outside the $95\%$ confidence interval [R1]; the two methods agree here [R1] [2 marks] (e) $(5.589,\,6.111)$ [A1]; $5.5$ is outside it [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A $(100-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval and a two-sided test at significance level $\alpha\%$ give the same decision about a hypothesized mean.

subtopic: Confidence interval for a mean difference
statement: Ten volunteers have their systolic blood pressure measured before and after a month of a low-salt diet. Before: 88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90, 86, 91, 83, 87. After: 85, 90, 80, 91, 81, 88, 84, 89, 80, 86. Assume the differences are normally distributed. (a) Find the mean and standard deviation $s_{n-1}$ of the differences (before $-$ after). [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean reduction in blood pressure. [3] (c) State what the interval suggests about whether the diet lowers blood pressure, and state one limitation of the study design. [2]
markscheme: (a) Differences: 3, 2, -1, 4, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1 [M1]; $\bar d=2.10$, $s_{n-1}=1.370$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t$-interval with $df=9$ [M1]: $(1.120,\,3.080)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) The interval is entirely positive (1.12 to 3.08) so there is evidence of a reduction [A1]; no control group, so other factors may explain the change [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For paired data, form the differences first, then treat them as a single sample.

subtopic: What does 95 percent confidence mean?
statement: This question investigates the meaning of a confidence interval. The masses (in grams) of cereal boxes from a factory are normally distributed with unknown mean $\mu$ and known standard deviation $12$. A quality inspector takes many independent random samples of size $n=36$ and, for each, constructs a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ using $\bar x\pm1.96\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$. (a) Find the margin of error of each interval. [2] (b) Show that $P(\bar X-1.96\sigma/\sqrt n<\mu<\bar X+1.96\sigma/\sqrt n)=0.95$. [3] (c) Twenty independent samples are taken, giving twenty intervals. Let $Y$ be the number of intervals that contain $\mu$. State the distribution of $Y$. [2] (d) Find the probability that all twenty intervals contain $\mu$, and the probability that at least two do not. [4] (e) Find the expected number of intervals that fail to contain $\mu$, and the standard deviation of that number. [3] (f) One sample has mean $\bar x=101.4$. Find its $95\%$ confidence interval. A colleague says there is a $95\%$ probability that $\mu$ lies in this interval. Explain why this wording is incorrect. [3] (g) The inspector wants the margin of error to be at most $1.5$ g. Find the smallest sample size needed. [3] (h) The factory also considers a $99\%$ interval. Find the sample size needed for a $99\%$ margin of error of at most $1.5$ g, and compare the two sample sizes. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1.96\times\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}}$ [M1] $=3.920$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ so $Z=\dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1)$ [M1]; $P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95$ [A1]; rearranging the inequality gives the stated result [AG] [3 marks] (c) $Y\sim B(20,0.95)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $P(Y=20)=0.95^{20}=0.3585$ [A1][A1]; $P(Y\leq18)=0.2642$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (e) Failures $\sim B(20,0.05)$ [A1]; mean $=1$ [A1]; $\sigma=\sqrt{20(0.05)(0.95)}=0.975$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $(97.48,\,105.32)$ [A1]; $\mu$ is a fixed number, not random [R1]; the $95\%$ refers to the long-run proportion of intervals, found this way, that contain $\mu$ [R1] [3 marks] (g) $1.96\times\dfrac{12}{\sqrt n}\leq1.5$ [M1]; $n\geq245.86$ [A1]; $n=246$ [A1] [3 marks] (h) $z=2.576$: $n\geq\left(\dfrac{2.576\times12}{1.5}\right)^2=424.69$ [M1][A1]; $n=425$, larger than for $95\%$ because more confidence needs more data [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A confidence interval is random before the sample is taken; the confidence level is the long-run proportion of such intervals that capture the fixed parameter. The number of capturing intervals among $k$ independent intervals is binomial.

subtopic: Tangent and normal using the product rule
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^{2} e^{x}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at $x=1$ and the coordinates of the point where the normal meets the $x$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) Using the product rule [M1][A1]: $f'(x)=x \left(x + 2\right) e^{x}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(1)=e$ [A1]; $f'(1)=3 e$ [A1]; $y-e=3 e(x-1)$ so $y=3 e x - 2 e$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Normal gradient $=-\dfrac{1}{3 e}=-\frac{1}{3 e}$ [A1]; $y=-\frac{x}{3 e} + \frac{1}{3 e} + e$ [A1]; at $y=0$, $x=1 + 3 e^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$ and simplify before substituting; the normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient.

subtopic: Tangent to a quotient at a given point
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\frac{e^{2 x}}{x + 1}$, for $x>-1$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [3] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at $x=0$ and the coordinates of the point where the normal meets the $x$-axis. [3]
markscheme: (a) Using the quotient rule [M1][A1]: $f'(x)=\frac{\left(2 x + 1\right) e^{2 x}}{x^{2} + 2 x + 1}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(0)=1$ [A1]; $f'(0)=1$ [A1]; $y-1=1(x-0)$ so $y=x + 1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Normal gradient $=-\dfrac{1}{1}=-1$ [A1]; $y=1 - x$ [A1]; at $y=0$, $x=1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a quotient $u/v$ use $(u'v-uv')/v^2$; evaluate each part at $x=0$ separately.

subtopic: Stationary points and inflection of a cubic
statement: A curve has equation $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=x^{3} - 6 x^{2} + 9 x + 2$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3 x^{2} - 12 x + 9$ [A1]; $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=1$ and $x=3$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=6 \left(x - 2\right)$ [A1]; at $x=1$, $f''=-6$ so a local maximum; at $x=3$, $f''=6$ so a local minimum [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(1,6)$; $(3,2)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=2$ [M1]; point $(2,4)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A point of inflection occurs where $f''$ changes sign, not merely where it is zero; here $f''$ is linear so it does change sign.

subtopic: Nature of stationary points using the second derivative
statement: Consider the function $f(x)=2 x^{3} - 9 x^{2} - 24 x + 10$. (a) Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x)=0$. [3] (b) Find $f''(x)$ and use it to determine the nature of each stationary point. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the stationary points. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=6 x^{2} - 18 x - 24$ [A1]; $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=-1$ and $x=4$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $f''(x)=6 \left(2 x - 3\right)$ [A1]; at $x=-1$, $f''=-30$ so a local maximum; at $x=4$, $f''=30$ so a local minimum [M1][A1] [3 marks] (c) $(-1,23)$; $(4,-102)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $f''(x)=0$ gives $x=\frac{3}{2}$ [M1]; point $(\frac{3}{2},- \frac{79}{2})$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: If $f''(c)<0$ at a stationary point the curve is concave down, so it is a local maximum.

subtopic: Maximum volume of an open box without a calculator
statement: A square sheet of cardboard of side $12$ cm has a square of side $x$ cm cut from each corner, and the sides are folded up to form an open box. (a) Show that the volume of the box is $V=x(12-2x)^2$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ and the value of $x$ for which $V$ is a maximum. [4] (c) Use the second derivative to verify that this value gives a maximum, and find the maximum volume. [3]
markscheme: (a) Base is a square of side $12-2x$ [A1]; height $x$ so $V=x(12-2x)^2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=4 x^{3} - 48 x^{2} + 144 x$, $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=12 x^{2} - 96 x + 144$ [A1]; $=0$ gives $x=2$ or $x=6$ [M1][A1]; reject $x=6$ as the base would vanish [R1] [4 marks] (c) $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=24 x - 96$, which is negative at $x=2$ [A1][R1]; $V_{max}=128$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The domain is $0<x<L/2$; reject any stationary value outside it, and confirm the maximum with the second derivative.

subtopic: Minimum surface area of a cylindrical can
statement: A closed cylindrical can has radius $r$ cm, height $h$ cm and volume $500$ cm$^3$. (a) Show that the total surface area is $A=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [3] (b) Use your calculator to find the value of $r$ that minimizes $A$, and the minimum area. [3] (c) Find the height at this radius and show that $h\approx2r$. [2] (d) Show algebraically that the minimum occurs when $h=2r$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\pi r^2h=500$ so $h=\dfrac{500}{\pi r^2}$ [M1]; $A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ [A1]; $=2\pi r^2+\dfrac{1000}{r}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) Differentiate or use the minimum function [M1]; $r=4.30$ [A1]; $A_{min}=348.7$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $h=8.60$ [A1]; $\dfrac{h}{r}=2.000\approx2$ [R1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=4\pi r-\dfrac{1000}{r^2}=0$ [M1] gives $4\pi r^3=1000=2\pi r^2h$ [A1] so $h=2r$ [AG] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $h$ using the volume first so that $A$ depends on one variable; the optimum shape of a closed can has height equal to its diameter.

subtopic: Profit and break-even points
statement: A bakery sells $x$ dozen cakes per day. Revenue is $R(x)=40x-0.5x^2$ dollars and the cost is $C(x)=80+12x$ dollars. (a) Find an expression for the profit $P(x)$ in dollars. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dP}{dx}$ and hence the value of $x$ that maximizes the profit. [3] (c) Find the maximum profit. [1] (d) Use your calculator to find the values of $x$ between which the company makes a profit. [2]
tips: Break-even happens at the two values of $x$ where profit is zero.

subtopic: Largest window with a semicircular top
statement: A window is made from a rectangle of width $2r$ meters and height $h$ meters, with a semicircle of radius $r$ on top. The total length of the frame (the perimeter) is $12$ m. (a) Show that $h=6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}$. [2] (b) Show that the area of the window is $A=12r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$. [3] (c) Find the value of $r$ that maximizes $A$, and the maximum area. [3] (d) Find the corresponding height $h$ and state the ratio $h:r$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter $=2h+2r+\pi r=12$ [M1] (bottom side, two vertical sides and semicircular arc); rearranging gives $h=6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $A=2rh+\dfrac12\pi r^2$ [M1]; $=2r\left(6-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}\right)+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$ [A1]; $=12r-2r^2-\pi r^2+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}=12r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=12-4r-\pi r=0$ [M1]; $r=\dfrac{12}{4+\pi}=1.680$ [A1]; $A_{max}=10.08$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $h=1.680$ [A1]; $h=r$, ratio $1:1$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the perimeter equation in terms of $r$ and $h$, solve for $h$, and substitute into the area; the optimal window has height of the rectangle equal to the radius.

subtopic: Rate of cooling of a liquid
statement: The temperature $T$ in $^\circ$C of a liquid $t$ minutes after it is poured into a cup is modeled by $T(t)=20+65e^{-0.08t}$ for $t\geq0$. (a) Write down the initial temperature and the temperature that the liquid approaches in the long run. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$ and the rate at which the liquid is cooling when $t=10$. [3] (c) Find the time at which the liquid is cooling at exactly $1.5^\circ$C per minute. [2] (d) Find the time at which the temperature is $55^\circ$C and the rate of change at that time. [3] (e) Show that $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.08(T-20)$ and explain what this says about the cooling rate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T(0)=85$ [A1]; $T\to20$ as $t\to\infty$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $T'(t)=-5.2e^{-0.08t}$ [A1][A1]; at $t=10$: $-2.337$ $^\circ$C per minute [A1] [3 marks] (c) $-5.2e^{-0.08t}=-1.5$ [M1]; $t=15.54$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $20+65e^{-0.08t}=55$ [M1]; $t=7.74$ [A1]; $T'=-2.800$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-5.2e^{-0.08t}=-0.08\left(65e^{-0.08t}\right)=-0.08(T-20)$ [AG]; the rate is proportional to the temperature difference from the surroundings [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Differentiate $e^{-0.08t}$ using the chain rule; the cooling rate is largest at the start and decreases as the liquid nears room temperature.

subtopic: Area of a triangle formed by a tangent and the axes
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$ for $x\geq0$. The tangent to the curve at the point $P$ where $x=3$ meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. The origin is $O$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent at $P$. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of $A$ and $B$. [2] (d) Find the area of triangle $OAB$. [2] (e) Use your calculator to find the values of $x$ for which the gradient of the curve is $-0.05$. [3]
tips: The tangent at a point has gradient $f'(a)$; intercepts come from setting $x=0$ and $y=0$ in its equation.

subtopic: Marginal cost, average cost and profit
statement: This question investigates the costs of producing $q$ items per day in a small factory. The total daily cost in dollars is $C(q)=0.01q^3-0.9q^2+30q+400$ for $0<q\leq80$. (a) Find the marginal cost $C'(q)$. [2] (b) Find the value of $q$ at which the marginal cost is least, and the least marginal cost. [3] (c) The average cost per item is $A(q)=\dfrac{C(q)}{q}$. Write down an expression for $A(q)$. [1] (d) Use your calculator to find the value of $q$ that minimizes the average cost, and the minimum average cost. [3] (e) Show that when $A(q)$ is a minimum, $C'(q)=A(q)$. [3] (f) Verify numerically that the marginal cost and the average cost agree at the value of $q$ from part (d). [2] (g) The revenue is $R(q)=45q-0.02q^2$. Find $P(q)=R(q)-C(q)$ and use your calculator to find the production level that maximizes the daily profit, and the maximum profit. [4] (h) Show that at the profit-maximizing level marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and state the sign of $P''$ there. [2]
tips: Average cost is minimized where marginal cost equals average cost; profit is maximized where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Check endpoints of the domain when optimizing on a closed interval.

subtopic: Exact area under a polynomial-exponential curve
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=3 x^{2} + e^{x}$. (a) Find $\int f(x)\,dx$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$. [3] (c) The curve passes through $(0,1)$. State, giving a reason, whether the region lies entirely above the $x$-axis. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int f(x)\,dx=x^{3} + e^{x}+c$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct term/part) [2 marks] (b) $\left[x^{3} + e^{x}\right]_{0}^{2}$ [M1]; $=e^{2} + 8-(1)$ [A1]; $=7 + e^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)>0$ on the interval, so the definite integral equals the area [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Integrate term by term: $\int e^x\,dx=e^x$; substitute the limits upper minus lower.

subtopic: Definite integral with a reciprocal term
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=4 x + \frac{3}{x}$ for $x>0$. (a) Find $\int f(x)\,dx$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact area of the region bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=1$ and $x=3$. [3] (c) The curve passes through $(1,7)$. State, giving a reason, whether the region lies entirely above the $x$-axis. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int f(x)\,dx=2 x^{2} + 3 \log{\left(x \right)}+c$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct term/part) [2 marks] (b) $\left[2 x^{2} + 3 \log{\left(x \right)}\right]_{1}^{3}$ [M1]; $=3 \log{\left(3 \right)} + 18-(2)$ [A1]; $=\log{\left(27 \right)} + 16$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)>0$ on the interval, so the definite integral equals the area [R1] [1 mark]
tips: $\int\dfrac1x\,dx=\ln|x|$; for exact answers leave $\ln$ terms unevaluated.

subtopic: Area enclosed by a parabola and a line
statement: The curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ have equations $f(x)=-x^{2} + 6 x$ and $g(x)=2 x$. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the region enclosed by the two curves. [4]
tips: The region between two curves has area $\int(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx$ between the intersection points.

subtopic: Exact volume of revolution about the x-axis
statement: The region is bounded by the curve $y=x + 1$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=3$. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed when the region between the curve, the $x$-axis, $x=0$ and $x=3$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Find the exact volume. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{3}y^2\,dx=\pi\int_{0}^{3}\left(x + 1\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $y^2=x^{2} + 2 x + 1$ [A1]; integrate [M1]; $V=21 \pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Square $y$ before integrating; the factor $\pi$ stays outside.

subtopic: Finding a function from its derivative and a point
statement: The gradient function of a curve is $f'(x)=6 x^{2} - 4 x + 2 e^{2 x}$ and the curve passes through $(0,5)$. Find $f(x)$. [4]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration; use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Area between an exponential and a line using a GDC
statement: The graphs of $f(x)=e^{\frac{x}{2}}$ and $g(x)=3 x - 1$ enclose a finite region. (a) Use your calculator to find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the two graphs intersect. [2] (b) Find the area of the region enclosed by the two graphs. [3] (c) Explain why it is not enough to evaluate $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\int_a^b g(x)\,dx$ without checking which function is greater. [1]
markscheme: (a) Solve $f(x)=g(x)$ [M1]: $x=0.841$ and $x=5.470$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Area $=\int_{0.841}^{5.470}|f(x)-g(x)|\,dx$ [M1][A1]; $=11.417$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) If the graphs swap order, the signed integrals partly cancel; the area uses upper minus lower on each section [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Sketch both graphs first so that you know which one is on top between the intersection points.

subtopic: Volume of a vase using a GDC
statement: A vase is modeled by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{x} e^{- \frac{x}{4}} + 0.5$, for $0\leq x\leq6$ (units in decimeters), about the $x$-axis. (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed by rotating the region about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Use your calculator to evaluate the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the radius of the solid at its widest point and the position at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{6}\left(\sqrt{x} e^{- \frac{x}{4}} + 0.5\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=28.33$ (units$^3$) [M1][A1] $\approx28.3$ [2 marks] (c) Use the maximum function [M1]; widest radius $1.358$ at $x=2.000$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the exact function (not a rounded copy) in the GDC integral; $V=\pi\int y^2dx$.

subtopic: Volume of a solid of revolution of an exponential-quadratic
statement: The region bounded by $y=\frac{x}{4} + 2 e^{- \frac{x}{3}}$, the axes and $x=5$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis (units are centimeters). (a) Write down an integral for the volume of the solid formed by rotating the region about the $x$-axis. [2] (b) Use your calculator to evaluate the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the radius of the solid at its widest point and the position at which it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $V=\pi\int_{0}^{5}\left(\frac{x}{4} + 2 e^{- \frac{x}{3}}\right)^2dx$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=40.39$ (units$^3$) [M1][A1] $\approx40.4$ [2 marks] (c) Use the maximum function [M1]; widest radius $2.000$ at $x=0.000$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Include the factor $\pi$; squaring $f$ first helps when entering it into the GDC.

subtopic: Trapezoidal rule from tabulated depth readings
statement: The depth $d$ meters of a river is measured at distances $x$ meters from one bank: $x=0,2,4,6,8,10$ with $d=0,3.2,5.9,7.4,6.8,3.1$ . (a) Use the trapezoidal rule with 5 intervals to estimate the cross-sectional area of the river. [3] (b) The river flows at an average speed of $0.8$ m/s. Estimate the volume of water passing per second. [2] (c) State, with a reason, whether the estimate is likely to be an underestimate or overestimate if the depth profile is concave down between readings. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{h}{2}\left(y_0+2(y_1+\dots+y_4)+y_5\right)$ with $h=2$ [M1][A1]; $=49.7$ m$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Flow $=0.8\times49.7$ [M1] $=39.76$ m$^3$/s [A1] [2 marks] (c) Underestimate [A1]; the chords of a concave-down curve lie below the curve, so the trapezia have less area [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The trapezoidal rule adds $h/2$ times (first + last + twice the rest); concavity tells you whether it overestimates or underestimates.

subtopic: Accumulated change from a rate of flow
statement: Water flows into a reservoir at a rate of $R(t)=40e^{-0.2t}+5t$ thousand liters per hour, where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight, for $0\leq t\leq12$. (a) Find the rate of flow at $t=0$ and at $t=10$. [2] (b) Find the total volume that enters the reservoir during the first $10$ hours, to the nearest thousand liters. [3] (c) Find the time at which the total volume that has entered first reaches $300$ thousand liters. [3] (d) Show that $R$ has a minimum value for $t>0$ and find the time at which it occurs. [3]
tips: The area under a rate-of-flow graph gives the total change; use the GDC definite integral and equation solver with the upper limit as the unknown.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=6t-4$ m s$^{-2}$. When $t=0$ the velocity is $-4$ m s$^{-1}$ and the displacement from the origin is $1$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement $s$ at time $t$, given that $s=1$ when $t=0$. [3] (c) Find the velocity and the displacement when $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the time(s), for $t>0$, at which the particle is momentarily at rest. [2]
tips: Integrate once for velocity and again for displacement, using each initial condition to find its constant.

subtopic: Particle with changing acceleration
statement: A particle $P$ moves along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds its acceleration is $a=12-6t$ m s$^{-2}$. When $t=0$, $v=-9$ m s$^{-1}$ and $s=2$ m. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ at time $t$. [3] (b) Find the displacement $s$ at time $t$, given that $s=2$ when $t=0$. [3] (c) Find the velocity and the displacement when $t=3$. [2] (d) Find the time(s), for $t>0$, at which the particle is momentarily at rest. [2]
tips: Velocity is the integral of acceleration; momentarily at rest means $v=0$ (take the positive root of the quadratic).

subtopic: Displacement versus total distance
statement: A particle moves in a straight line with velocity $v=t^2-6t+8$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq5$. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction in the interval given. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in this time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=0$: $t=2$, $t=4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{5}v\,dt=\frac{20}{3}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Split the integral at the direction changes [M1]: $\frac{20}{3}$, $-\frac{4}{3}$, $\frac{4}{3}$ [A1]; total distance $=\frac{28}{3}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Distance is the integral of $|v|$; split the interval where the velocity changes sign and add the absolute values.

subtopic: Total distance for a cubic velocity
statement: The velocity of a particle on a straight line is $v=(t-1)(t-2)(t-4)$ m s$^{-1}$, for $0\leq t\leq5$. (a) Find the times at which the particle changes direction in the interval given. [2] (b) Find the displacement of the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in this time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=0$: $t=1$, $t=2$, $t=4$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int_0^{5}v\,dt=-\frac{5}{12}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Split the integral at the direction changes [M1]: $-\frac{37}{12}$, $\frac{5}{12}$, $-\frac{8}{3}$, $\frac{59}{12}$ [A1]; total distance $=\frac{133}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Sketch $v$ first: the sign pattern tells you on which intervals the particle moves forward or backward.

subtopic: Velocity with an exponential model
statement: A particle moves along a line with velocity $v=6e^{-t/2}$ m s$^{-1}$, $t\geq0$. (a) Find the acceleration at time $t$ and its value at $t=0$. [2] (b) Find the exact distance traveled between $t=0$ and $t=2\ln2$. [3] (c) Find the limit of the displacement as $t\to\infty$. [2]
tips: $e^{-t/2}$ decreases but never reaches zero, so the particle never stops in finite time, yet its total displacement is finite.

subtopic: Distance and speed from a displacement function
statement: A particle moves in a straight line so that its displacement from the origin at time $t$ seconds is $s(t)=t^{3} - \frac{15 t^{2}}{2} + 12 t + 3$ meters. (a) Find the velocity and acceleration when $t=2$. [3] (b) Find the times in the interval $0<t<6$ at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the first 6 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle in the interval $0\leq t\leq6$ and when it occurs. [3]
markscheme: (a) $v=s'(t)=3 t^{2} - 15 t + 12$ [A1]; $a=v'(t)=6 t - 15$ [A1]; $v(2)=-6.000$, $a(2)=-3.000$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $v=0$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=1.000$, $t=4.000$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\int_0^{6}|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1]; $=45.000$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximize $|v|$ on the interval (check endpoints) [M1]; greatest speed $30.000$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] at $t=6.000$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total distance needs $|v|$: integrate on each interval where $v$ keeps one sign, or use the GDC integral of $|v|$.

subtopic: Particle with an oscillating displacement
statement: The displacement of a particle from a fixed point is $s(t)=2 t e^{- \frac{t}{2}} \sin{\left(t \right)} + 1$ meters at time $t$ seconds (radians for the sine). (a) Find the velocity and acceleration when $t=2$. [3] (b) Find the times in the interval $0<t<6$ at which the particle is at rest. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the first 6 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest speed of the particle in the interval $0\leq t\leq6$ and when it occurs. [3]
