markscheme: (a) $v=s'(t)=\left(-t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) e^{- \frac{t}{2}}$ [A1]; $a=v'(t)=\frac{\left(-3 t \sin{\left(t \right)} - 4 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 4 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 8 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) e^{- \frac{t}{2}}}{2}$ [A1]; $v(2)=-0.612$, $a(2)=-1.673$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Solve $v=0$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=1.669$, $t=4.444$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Distance $=\int_0^{6}|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1]; $=4.575$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximize $|v|$ on the interval (check endpoints) [M1]; greatest speed $1.372$ m s$^{-1}$ [A1] at $t=2.872$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the calculator to radian mode; solve $v=0$ numerically and integrate $|v|$ for the distance.

subtopic: Stopping distance of a decelerating vehicle
statement: A vehicle enters a gravel runway with velocity $v=25e^{-0.3t}$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after entering. (a) Find an expression for the displacement from the start after $t$ seconds. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in the first $3$ seconds. [2] (c) Show that the vehicle can never travel further than 83.33 m, and find how long it takes to travel 50 m. [4] (d) Find the acceleration when $t=0$ and when $t=5$. [3]
tips: Because the velocity never reaches zero, the displacement approaches a finite limit; use $e^{-kt}\to0$.

subtopic: Boat slowing after the engine is switched off
statement: After the engine of a boat is switched off, its velocity is modeled by $v=12e^{-0.15t}$ m s$^{-1}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after switch-off. (a) Find an expression for the displacement from the start after $t$ seconds. [3] (b) Find the distance traveled in the first $3$ seconds. [2] (c) Show that the boat can never travel further than 80 m, and find how long it takes to travel 60 m. [4] (d) Find the acceleration when $t=0$ and when $t=5$. [3]
tips: Find the limit of the displacement first to decide which target distances are reachable.

subtopic: Two particles on the same line
statement: Particles $A$ and $B$ move on the same straight line. Their displacements from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds are $s_A=t^2-4t+3$ and $s_B=\dfrac12t^2-t+1$, in meters, for $t\geq0$. (a) Find the initial positions of $A$ and $B$ and their initial velocities. [3] (b) Find the times at which the particles are at the same position. [3] (c) Find the speeds of the two particles at the first of these times. [3] (d) Find the maximum distance between the particles in the interval between their meetings, and describe their relative motion. [3]
tips: Two particles meet when their displacements are equal; relative velocity is the difference of the velocities.

subtopic: Particle with a sinusoidal velocity
statement: The velocity of a particle moving on a straight line is $v=5\sin(0.8t)-1$ m s$^{-1}$ for $0\leq t\leq8$, where $t$ is in seconds. Use radians. (a) Find the times at which the particle is at rest in this interval. [3] (b) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting point at $t=8$. [2] (c) Find the total distance traveled in the 8 seconds. [3] (d) Find the greatest magnitude of the acceleration and the first time it occurs. [3] (e) State the period of the motion of the velocity and the first time after $t=0$ at which the velocity is again $-1$ m s$^{-1}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $5\sin(0.8t)=1$ [M1]; $t=0.252$ [A1]; $t=3.675$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\int_0^8v\,dt$ [M1] $=-7.957$ m [A1] [2 marks] (c) Split at the rest times: $\int|v|\,dt$ [M1][A1] $=25.605$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a=4\cos(0.8t)$ [A1]; greatest magnitude $4$ m s$^{-2}$ [A1] at $t=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{0.8}=7.854$ s [A1]; $5\sin(0.8t)-1=-1$ gives $\sin(0.8t)=0$ [M1]; first positive time $t=3.927$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A velocity that is sinusoidal has an acceleration that is its derivative; remember the chain-rule factor $0.8$ when differentiating.

subtopic: Inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix and solving a system
statement: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (d) State the value of $k$ for which the matrix $A$ with its entry $2$ replaced by $k$ is singular. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=3(2)-(1)(5)=1$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{1}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=2$ [A1]; $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Singular when $\det=0$: $3k-(1)(5)=0$ [M1]; $k=\frac{5}{3}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For a $2\times2$ matrix, swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant.

subtopic: Using the inverse matrix to solve linear equations
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det A$. [1] (b) Find $A^{-1}$. [2] (c) Hence solve $A\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 13 \end{pmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (d) State the value of $k$ for which the matrix $A$ with its entry $4$ replaced by $k$ is singular. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\det A=2(4)-(-3)(1)=11$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{11}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{4}{11} & \frac{3}{11} \\ - \frac{1}{11} & \frac{2}{11} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=\frac{43}{11}$ [A1]; $y=\frac{25}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) Singular when $\det=0$: $2k-(-3)(1)=0$ [M1]; $k=-\frac{3}{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ gives $\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$; multiply the inverse on the left.

subtopic: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and a matrix power
statement: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$ and use it to find $A^{3}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(7)\lambda+(10)=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=2$ or $5$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=2$: $\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; for $\lambda=5$: $\mathbf{v}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=PD^{3}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $A^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Find eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial, then each eigenvector from $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$; powers use $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$.

subtopic: Diagonalizing a symmetric matrix
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [3] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$ and use it to find $A^{4}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(7)\lambda+(6)=0$ [M1][A1]; $\lambda=1$ or $6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) For $\lambda=1$: $\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; for $\lambda=6$: $\mathbf{v}_2=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (any non-zero multiples) [3 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{4}=PD^{4}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $A^{4}=\begin{pmatrix} 1037 & 518 \\ 518 & 260 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a symmetric matrix the eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain and steady state by hand
statement: Each month, $20\%$ of customers of phone company $A$ switch to $B$, and $30\%$ of customers of $B$ switch to $A$. Everyone else stays. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$, with columns giving the probabilities of moving from each state. [2] (b) Find the probability that a company A user is still a company A user after two changes (that is, the entry of $T^2$). [3] (c) Find the long-run proportion in each state by solving $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with $s_1+s_2=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{1}{5} & \frac{7}{10} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each column) [2 marks] (b) $T^2=\begin{pmatrix} \frac{7}{10} & \frac{9}{20} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{11}{20} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; probability $=\frac{7}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $(1-a)s_1+bs_2=s_1$ gives $as_1=bs_2$ [M1]; with $s_1+s_2=1$: $s_1=\frac{3}{5}$ [A1], $s_2=\frac{2}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A steady state satisfies $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$; the long-run proportions are in the ratio of the opposite switching probabilities.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for weather
statement: The weather in a town each day is sunny, cloudy or rainy. The transition matrix $T$ (columns = today's weather in the order sunny, cloudy, rainy) is $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Verify that $T$ is a valid transition matrix and state what the $(2,1)$ entry represents. [2] (b) Find the distribution after 5 steps, starting from $\mathbf{p}_0=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (c) Find the steady state vector. [3] (d) Explain why the long-run distribution does not depend on the starting distribution. [1] (e) Find the smallest $n$ such that the probability of being in the first state after $n$ steps (starting from the first state) is within $0.01$ of its long-run value. [3]
markscheme: (a) Each column sums to $1$ [A1]; the $(2,1)$ entry is the probability of moving from sunny to cloudy in one step [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{p}_{5}=T^{5}\mathbf{p}_0$ [M1]; $=\begin{pmatrix} 0.4737 \\ 0.3131 \\ 0.2133 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) Solve $T\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{s}$ with sum $1$ (eigenvector for $\lambda=1$) [M1]; $\mathbf{s}=\begin{pmatrix} 0.4634 \\ 0.3171 \\ 0.2195 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) All entries of some power of $T$ are positive (a regular chain), so $T^n$ converges to a matrix with identical columns equal to $\mathbf{s}$ [R1] [1 mark] (e) Compute $T^n\mathbf{e}_1$ for increasing $n$ [M1]; $n=6$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each column of a transition matrix sums to 1; a steady state is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1, scaled to sum to 1.

subtopic: Encoding and decoding with a 3 by 3 matrix
statement: A message is coded by replacing letters by numbers ($A=1,B=2,\dots,Z=26$) and splitting into blocks of three numbers. Each block, written as a column vector $\mathbf{m}$, is encoded as $K\mathbf{m}$, where $K=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\det K$ and state why $K$ can be used for coding. [2] (b) Encode the block $\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (c) Use your calculator to find $K^{-1}$ (give exact fractions). [2] (d) The received coded blocks are $\begin{pmatrix} 108 \\ 65 \\ 97 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 84 \\ 63 \\ 87 \end{pmatrix}$. Decode them, and write the letters. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det K=-8$ [A1]; non-zero so $K^{-1}$ exists and the message can be recovered [R1] [2 marks] (b) $K\mathbf{m}=\begin{pmatrix} 57 \\ 30 \\ 53 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $K^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} - \frac{3}{8} & - \frac{1}{8} & \frac{5}{8} \\ - \frac{1}{8} & \frac{5}{8} & - \frac{1}{8} \\ \frac{5}{8} & - \frac{1}{8} & - \frac{3}{8} \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $K^{-1}$ times each block [M1]: $\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 15 \\ 23 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 18 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1]; letters L, O, W, O, R, L [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Decoding multiplies by the inverse matrix; check that your decoded numbers lie between 1 and 26.

subtopic: Two lakes exchanging a pollutant (discrete model)
statement: Two connected lakes $P$ and $Q$ hold pollutant masses $p_n$ and $q_n$ (in kg) at the start of week $n$. Each week $15\%$ of the pollutant in $P$ moves to $Q$, and $20\%$ of the pollutant in $Q$ moves to $P$. Initially $p_0=120$ and $q_0=40$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} p_{n+1} \\ q_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}=T\begin{pmatrix} p_n \\ q_n \end{pmatrix}$. [2] (b) Find the masses of pollutant in each lake after 4 weeks. [3] (c) Show that the total mass of pollutant is constant. [1] (d) Find the eigenvalues of $T$ and the eigenvector for $\lambda=1$. [3] (e) Find the long-run mass in each lake. [2] (f) Show that the deviation from the long-run state decays by a factor of $0.65$ each week, and find after how many weeks the mass in $P$ is within $1$ kg of its long-run value. [3]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.85 & 0.20 \\ 0.15 & 0.80 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (b) $T^4\begin{pmatrix}120\\40\end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $p_4=96.53$ [A1]; $q_4=63.47$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Each column of $T$ sums to $1$, so $p_{n+1}+q_{n+1}=p_n+q_n$ [R1] [1 mark] (d) $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=0.65$ [A1][A1]; eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) Total $=160$ kg shared in ratio $4:3$ [M1]: $p\to91.43$, $q\to68.57$ kg [A1] [2 marks] (f) Second eigenvalue $0.65$ [A1]; $|p_n-91.43|=|28.57|(0.65)^n<1$ [M1]; $n=8$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The second eigenvalue controls how quickly the system approaches the steady state; the first (equal to 1) reflects conservation of total mass.

subtopic: Exponential decay with a given half-life
statement: A radioactive sample has mass $M$ milligrams at time $t$ hours. Initially the mass is $80$ mg and the mass halves every $6$ hours. (a) Show that the model can be written as $M=80e^{-kt}$ where $k=\dfrac{\ln2}{6}$. [3] (b) Find the mass remaining after 18 hours. [2] (c) Find, in terms of $\ln$, the time for the mass to fall to $16$. [3]
markscheme: (a) After 6 hours the mass is $\dfrac{80}{2}$ so $80e^{-6k}=\dfrac{80}{2}$ [M1]; $e^{-6k}=\dfrac12$ [A1]; $k=\dfrac{\ln2}{6}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) 18 hours is three half-lives [M1]; $80\times\left(\dfrac12\right)^3=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $80e^{-kt}=16$ [M1]; $e^{-kt}=\dfrac15$ [A1]; $t=\dfrac{\ln5}{k}=\dfrac{6\ln5}{\ln2}$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Three half-lives reduce the mass by a factor of $2^3$; for other times use logarithms.

subtopic: Half-life and time to reach a fraction
statement: The mass $M$ grams of a drug in the body $t$ days after a dose follows an exponential decay model. The initial mass is $200$ g and the half-life is $12$ days. (a) Show that the model can be written as $M=200e^{-kt}$ where $k=\dfrac{\ln2}{12}$. [3] (b) Find the mass remaining after 36 days. [2] (c) Find, in terms of $\ln$, the time for the mass to fall to $40$. [3]
markscheme: (a) After 12 days the mass is $\dfrac{200}{2}$ so $200e^{-12k}=\dfrac{200}{2}$ [M1]; $e^{-12k}=\dfrac12$ [A1]; $k=\dfrac{\ln2}{12}$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) 36 days is three half-lives [M1]; $200\times\left(\dfrac12\right)^3=25$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $200e^{-kt}=40$ [M1]; $e^{-kt}=\dfrac15$ [A1]; $t=\dfrac{\ln5}{k}=\dfrac{12\ln5}{\ln2}$ days [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $e^{-kt}=\text{fraction remaining}$ and take natural logarithms of both sides.

subtopic: Sinusoidal model with exact values
statement: A point on the rim of a water wheel is at height $h(t)=5+4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$ meters above the water after $t$ seconds. (a) Write down the greatest and the least height of the point, and the period of the motion. [3] (b) Find the height at $t=1$, $t=3$ and $t=5$ exactly. [3] (c) Solve $h(t)=3$ for $0\leq t\leq12$, giving exact answers. [3]
markscheme: (a) Greatest $=5+4=9$ m [A1]; least $=5-4=1$ m [A1]; period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=12$ s [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h(1)=5+4\sin\dfrac\pi6=7$ [A1]; $h(3)=5+4\sin\dfrac\pi2=9$ [A1]; $h(5)=5+4\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}=-\dfrac12$ [M1]; $\dfrac{\pi t}6=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ [A1]; $t=7$ and $t=11$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The amplitude is the coefficient of the sine, the midline is the constant term, and the period is $2\pi$ divided by the coefficient of $t$.

subtopic: Maximum of a quadratic model by completing the square
statement: A farmer uses $60$ m of fencing to make a rectangular pen against a long straight wall, so only three sides need fencing. The two sides perpendicular to the wall have length $x$ meters. (a) Show that the area of the pen is $A=x(60-2x)$. [2] (b) By completing the square, or otherwise, find the maximum area and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [4] (c) State the dimensions of the pen and write down the domain of $x$ for the model to make sense. [2]
markscheme: (a) Length parallel to wall $=60-2x$ [A1]; $A=x(60-2x)$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $A=-2x^2+60x=-2(x-15)^2+450$ [M1][A1]; maximum area $450$ m$^2$ [A1] at $x=15$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $15$ m by $30$ m [A1]; $0<x<30$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complete the square by factoring $-2$ from the $x$ terms; the vertex gives the maximum value of a downward parabola.

subtopic: Inverse variation model
statement: The time $t$ hours taken to fill a pool using $n$ identical pumps is modeled by $t=\dfrac{k}{n}$. With $4$ pumps the pool fills in $9$ hours. (a) Find the value of $k$. [1] (b) Find the time taken with $6$ pumps, and the number of pumps needed to fill the pool in $2$ hours. [3] (c) State the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of $t$ against $n$ and interpret the horizontal one. [2]
markscheme: (a) $9=\dfrac k4$ so $k=36$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $t=\dfrac{36}{6}=6$ hours [A1]; $2=\dfrac{36}{n}$ [M1] so $n=18$ pumps [A1] [3 marks] (c) $n=0$ and $t=0$ [A1]; the time approaches $0$ as more pumps are used but never reaches it [R1] [2 marks]
tips: An inverse variation $t=k/n$ has hyperbola graphs; use one data point to find the constant.

subtopic: Logistic growth of a population
statement: The number of members $N$ of an online group $t$ months after it was founded is modeled by $N=\dfrac{800}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}$, for $t\geq0$. (a) Find the initial number of members, and the limiting number of members as $t\to\infty$. [3] (b) Find the number of members after 6 months, to the nearest whole number. [2] (c) Find the time at which the group reaches $400$ members. [2] (d) Find the time taken for the membership to reach $90\%$ of its limiting value. [2] (e) Use your calculator to find the time at which the membership is growing fastest, and state that growth rate. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N(0)=\dfrac{800}{16}=50$ [A1]; as $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to0$ so $N\to800$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $N(6)=458.0\approx458$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{800}{1+15e^{-0.5t}}=400$ [M1]; $t=5.42$ months [A1] [2 marks] (d) $N=720$: $t=9.81$ months [M1][A1] [2 marks] (e) Maximum of $N'(t)$ [M1]; $t=5.42$ months [A1] (when $N=400$); rate $100.0$ members per month [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A logistic curve has an inflection point at half the carrying capacity, where the growth rate is greatest.

subtopic: A sinusoidal tide model
statement: The depth $D$ meters of water in a harbor is modeled by $D(t)=a+c\sin(b(t-1.6))$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight. The maximum depth is $7.2$ m, the minimum depth is $1.4$ m, and the time between successive high tides is $12.4$ hours. (a) Find the values of $a$, $c$ and $b$. [4] (b) Find the depth at $t=4$. [2] (c) A boat needs a depth of at least $5$ m. Find the times between midnight and midnight the next day (24 hours) during which the boat can enter the harbor, giving answers to the nearest minute. [4] (d) Find the time of the first high tide after midnight, and the rate at which the depth is changing at $t=4$ (give sign and units). [3]
tips: For $D=a+c\sin(b(t-d))$: $a$ is the midline, $c$ the amplitude, $b=2\pi/\text{period}$ and $d$ the horizontal shift; use the GDC to solve for times and check radian mode.

subtopic: Comparing a linear and an exponential price plan
statement: A cloud storage company offers two plans. Plan $A$ costs $C_A=18+0.9g$ dollars per month for $g$ gigabytes stored. Plan $B$ costs $C_B=6(1.35)^g$ dollars per month for $g$ gigabytes, for $g\geq0$. (a) Find the cost of each plan for $g=5$. [2] (b) Use your calculator to find the value of $g$ for which the two plans cost the same. [3] (c) State the range of $g$ for which plan $B$ is cheaper than plan $A$. [2] (d) Explain why plan $B$ would not be sensible for a very large amount of storage. [1]
markscheme: (a) $C_A=22.50$ [A1]; $C_B=26.90$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Intersection of the graphs [M1]: $g=4.311$ [A1]; cost $\$21.88$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Plan $B$ is cheaper for $0\leq g<4.311$ [A1]; plan $A$ is cheaper for $g>4.311$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $C_B$ grows exponentially, so it eventually exceeds the linear $C_A$ by a huge amount [R1] [1 mark]
tips: At an intersection the two cost functions are equal; compare the sign of the difference on each side to decide which plan is cheaper.

subtopic: Depreciation: exponential or linear model
statement: A delivery van bought for \$32\,000 loses value. Model 1 says its value after $t$ years is $V_1=32000(0.85)^t$ dollars. Model 2 says it loses a constant $10\%$ of its original value each year, so $V_2=32000-3200t$. (a) Find the value of the van after $4$ years according to each model. [2] (b) Find the time for the value to fall below \$10\,000 according to each model. [4] (c) State, with a reason, which model predicts the greater value after $10$ years. [2] (d) Find the time $t>0$ at which the two models predict the same value. [3] (e) Explain why model 2 is unreasonable for $t>10$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $V_1=16704.20$ [A1]; $V_2=19200$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Model 1: $32000(0.85)^t=10000$ [M1]; $t=7.16$ years [A1]; model 2: $32000-3200t=10000$ [M1]; $t=6.88$ years [A1] [4 marks] (c) $V_1(10)=6300$, $V_2(10)=0$ [A1]; model 1 is greater because an exponential decay never reaches zero [R1] [2 marks] (d) Solve $32000(0.85)^t=32000-3200t$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=6.552$ [A1]; the trivial solution $t=0$ (the purchase price) is not counted [R1] [3 marks] (e) It gives a negative value after $10$ years [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A constant percentage loss gives a geometric (exponential) model; a constant dollar loss gives a linear model, which becomes negative eventually.

subtopic: Two Ferris wheels: modeling with cosine functions
statement: This question investigates the motion of riders on two Ferris wheels. The first wheel has radius $30$ m, its centre is $35$ m above the ground, and it makes one complete revolution every $20$ minutes. A rider on this wheel is at the lowest point of the wheel at time $t=0$ minutes. (a) Show that the height $h_1$ of the rider above the ground at time $t$ is modeled by $h_1=35-30\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$. [3] (b) Find the rider's height at $t=6$ minutes. [2] (c) Find the times in the first revolution during which the rider is at least $50$ m above the ground. [3] (d) Find the percentage of the revolution for which the rider is at least $50$ m high. [2] (e) Find $\dfrac{dh_1}{dt}$. Hence find the rate at which the rider's height is changing at $t=5$, and the greatest rate of increase of height. [4] (f) A second wheel has radius $25$ m, centre $30$ m above the ground, one revolution every $15$ minutes, and its rider also starts at the lowest point at $t=0$. Write down $h_2$ and use your calculator to find the first time after $t=0$ that the two riders are at the same height. [4] (g) Find the speed of the first rider around the rim, in m per minute. [2] (h) Explain why the greatest rate of change of height equals the rim speed, and state one assumption of the model. [2]
markscheme: (a) Midline $35$ and amplitude $30$ [A1]; lowest point at $t=0$ so a negative cosine [R1]; $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{20}=\dfrac\pi{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h_1(6)=35-30\cos(0.6\pi)=44.27$ m [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $h_1=50$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=6.667$ and $t=13.333$ [A1]; the rider is at least $50$ m high for $6.67\leq t\leq13.33$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{6.667}{20}\times100=33.3\%$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dh_1}{dt}=3\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$ [A1][A1]; at $t=5$: $3\pi=9.425$ m per minute [A1]; greatest rate $3\pi$ m per minute at $t=5$ [A1] [4 marks] (f) $h_2=30-25\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi t}{15}\right)$ [A1]; solve $h_1=h_2$ [M1]; first time $t=7.312$ min [A1]; height $=54.92$ m [A1] [4 marks] (g) Speed $=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi(30)}{20}=3\pi=9.425$ m per minute [M1][A1] [2 marks] (h) The vertical speed is largest when the rider moves vertically, i.e. at the level of the centre [R1]; the wheel turns at constant speed (or the rider is a point on the rim) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A cosine model starting at a minimum uses $-\cos$; differentiate with the chain rule and compare the derivative's amplitude to the speed around the rim.

subtopic: Arc length and sector area in radians
statement: The points $A$ and $B$ lie on a circle with centre $O$ and radius $12$ cm. The angle $AOB=\dfrac\pi3$ radians. (a) Find the exact length of the arc $AB$. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the sector $OAB$. [2] (c) Find the exact perimeter of the sector. [1] (d) Find the exact area of the segment formed by the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s=r\theta=12\times\frac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=4 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\dfrac12r^2\theta=\dfrac12(12)^2\frac{\pi}{3}$ [M1] $=24 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2r+s=2(12)+4 \pi=4 \pi + 24$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Triangle area $=\dfrac12r^2\sin\theta=\dfrac12(12)^2\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=36 \sqrt{3}$ [M1][A1]; segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $=-36 \sqrt{3} + 24 \pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use radians for the arc length and sector formulas; the segment is the sector minus the triangle $OAB$.

subtopic: Segment area using radians
statement: A circle has centre $O$ and radius $8$ cm. Chord $AB$ subtends an angle $\dfrac\pi2$ at the centre. (a) Find the exact length of the arc $AB$. [2] (b) Find the exact area of the sector $OAB$. [2] (c) Find the exact perimeter of the sector. [1] (d) Find the exact area of the segment formed by the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $s=r\theta=8\times\frac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $=4 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $A=\dfrac12r^2\theta=\dfrac12(8)^2\frac{\pi}{2}$ [M1] $=16 \pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2r+s=2(8)+4 \pi=4 \pi + 16$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Triangle area $=\dfrac12r^2\sin\theta=\dfrac12(8)^2\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=32$ [M1][A1]; segment $=$ sector $-$ triangle $=-32 + 16 \pi$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For a right angle at the centre the triangle area is $\frac12r^2$.

subtopic: Exact solutions of a trigonometric equation
statement: A student models the phase angle $x$ of a rotating arm with the equation below, where $x$ is measured in radians. Solve the equation $2\sin x=\sqrt3$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$, giving exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\sin x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [M1]; reference angle $\dfrac\pi3$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1]; second solution $x=\pi-\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [M1][A1] [5 marks]
tips: Find the reference angle, then use the symmetry of the sine curve: $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$.

subtopic: Equation involving cosine and a transformed angle
statement: A technician writes the following condition for a rotating sensor, with $x$ in radians. Solve the equation $2\cos(2x)=-1$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$, giving exact answers. [5]
markscheme: $\cos2x=-\dfrac12$ [M1]; $2x=\dfrac{2\pi}3,\dfrac{4\pi}3,\dfrac{8\pi}3,\dfrac{10\pi}3$ (extended range $0\leq2x\leq4\pi$) [M1][A1]; $x=\dfrac\pi3,\dfrac{2\pi}3,\dfrac{4\pi}3,\dfrac{5\pi}3$ [A1][A1] (A1 for each correct pair) [5 marks]
tips: Because the angle is $2x$, solve over the longer interval $0\leq 2x\leq4\pi$ and then divide by $2$.

subtopic: A quadratic in sine without a calculator
statement: The vertical displacement ratio of a swinging gate satisfies the equation below, where $x$ is in radians. Solve the equation $2\sin^2x-\sin x-1=0$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$, giving exact answers. [5]
markscheme: Let $s=\sin x$: $2s^2-s-1=0$ [M1]; $(2s+1)(s-1)=0$ [A1]; $\sin x=-\dfrac12$ or $\sin x=1$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{7\pi}6,\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ [A1] and $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Treat $\sin x$ as a single variable to factorize; check each value lies in $[-1,1]$.

subtopic: Reading amplitude, period and phase shift
statement: Consider the function $f(x)=3\sin\left(2x-\dfrac\pi3\right)+1$. (a) Write down the amplitude, the period and the midline. [3] (b) Find the maximum and minimum values of $f$ and the smallest positive $x$ at which the maximum occurs. [3] (c) Describe the horizontal shift of the graph of $y=3\sin2x+1$ that gives the graph of $f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $3$ [A1]; period $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ [A1]; midline $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Maximum $4$, minimum $-2$ [A1]; $2x-\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f(x)=3\sin2\left(x-\dfrac\pi6\right)+1$ [M1]; shift right by $\dfrac\pi6$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rewrite $2x-\pi/3$ as $2(x-\pi/6)$ to read the horizontal shift correctly.

subtopic: A sector, its angle and the segment area
statement: A circular sector $OAB$ has radius $r=9$ cm and perimeter $36$ cm. (a) Find the length of the arc $AB$ and the angle $AOB$ in radians. [3] (b) Find the area of the sector. [2] (c) Find the area of the triangle $OAB$ and the area of the segment, to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the length of the chord $AB$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Perimeter $=2r+s$ so $s=36-18=18$ cm [M1][A1]; $\theta=\dfrac sr=\dfrac{18}{9}=2$ radians [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12r^2\theta=\dfrac12(81)(2)=81$ cm$^2$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Triangle $=\dfrac12(81)\sin2=36.827$ [M1][A1]; segment $=81-36.827=44.17$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $AB=2r\sin\dfrac\theta2=18\sin1=15.146$ cm [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Set the calculator to radians; the chord length is $2r\sin(\theta/2)$ (or use the cosine rule).

subtopic: Sinusoidal model of daylight hours
statement: The number of hours of daylight $y$ in a northern city is modeled by a cosine function of the day number $t$ ($t=0$ is January 1). The longest day has $15.8$ hours and occurs on day $172$. The shortest has $8.2$ hours. (a) Show that the model $y=d+a\cos(b(t-c))$ can have $a=3.8$, $d=12$. [2] (b) Find the values of $b$ and $c$, given that the period is 365 days and the maximum occurs at $t=172$. [2] (c) Find the predicted daylight (hours) at $t=100$. [2] (d) Find the times in one period ($0\leq t\leq365$) when the daylight (hours) is 10. [3]
tips: The midline is the mean of the maximum and minimum; the amplitude is half their difference. Check radians mode.

subtopic: Cosine model of the temperature of a greenhouse
statement: The temperature $y^\circ$C in a greenhouse over a day is modeled by a cosine function of the time $t$ hours after midnight. The maximum temperature $31$ occurs at $t=15$ and the minimum $17$ occurs $12$ hours earlier. (a) Show that the model $y=d+a\cos(b(t-c))$ can have $a=7$, $d=24$. [2] (b) Find the values of $b$ and $c$, given that the period is 24 hours and the maximum occurs at $t=15$. [2] (c) Find the predicted temperature at $t=9$. [2] (d) Find the times in one period ($0\leq t\leq24$) when the temperature is 26. [3]
tips: The time between a maximum and the next minimum is half a period.

subtopic: Solving a trigonometric equation graphically
statement: Let $f(x)=3\sin2x+1$ and $g(x)=0.5\cos x$, for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$. (a) Write down the range of $f$ and the period of $f$. [2] (b) Use your calculator to solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (c) Hence solve $f(x)>g(x)$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$. [3] (d) Find the greatest value of $f(x)-g(x)$ on the interval and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Range $[-2,4]$ [A1]; period $\pi$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Solve on the GDC (radians) [M1]: $x=1.757$, $x=2.883$, $x=4.869$, $x=6.199$ [A2] (award A1 for at least three correct) [3 marks] (c) Graph of $f$ above that of $g$ [M1]: $0\leq x<1.757$; $2.883<x<4.869$; $6.199<x\leq2\pi$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Maximum of the difference [M1]: $4.359$ at $x=3.898$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: List all solutions in $[0,2\pi]$ by examining the intersections on a sketch; solve inequalities from the graph.

subtopic: Alternating voltage modeled by a sine function
statement: The voltage $V$ volts across a mains circuit at time $t$ seconds is modeled by $V=325\sin(100\pi t)$. (a) Find the period of the voltage and the frequency in cycles per second. [3] (b) Find the voltage at $t=0.003$ s. [2] (c) Find the first two times after $t=0$ at which the voltage is $200$ volts. [3] (d) Find the length of time in one cycle for which the voltage is above $200$ volts, and the percentage of the cycle that this represents. [3] (e) Find the greatest rate at which the voltage changes, with units. [2]
markscheme: (a) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{100\pi}=0.02$ s [A1][A1]; frequency $=\dfrac1{0.02}=50$ Hz [A1] [3 marks] (b) $V=262.93$ volts [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $325\sin(100\pi t)=200$ [M1]: $t=0.00211$ s [A1] and $t=0.00789$ s [A1] [3 marks] (d) Duration $=0.00578$ s [M1][A1]; $\dfrac{0.00578}{0.02}=28.9\%$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $V'=32500\pi\cos(100\pi t)$, greatest value $32500\pi=102102$ volts per second [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: The coefficient of $t$ gives the angular frequency; the period is $2\pi$ divided by it and the frequency is the reciprocal of the period.

subtopic: A mass on a spring with a phase shift
statement: A mass on a spring has displacement $x$ centimeters from its rest position given by $x=12\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9\right)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. (a) State the amplitude and the period of the motion. [2] (b) Find the initial displacement, to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the first time at which the mass is at its greatest positive displacement. [3] (d) Find all times in the first two periods ($0\leq t\leq3.2$) at which the displacement is $6$ cm. [3] (e) Find the speed of the mass when $t=0.5$ s. [2]
markscheme: (a) Amplitude $12$ cm [A1]; period $1.6$ s [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x(0)=12\cos0.9=7.459$ cm [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Maximum when $\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9=2\pi$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac{(2\pi-0.9)(1.6)}{2\pi}=1.371$ s [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve $x=6$ on the GDC [M1]: $t=0.037$, $t=1.104$, $t=1.637$, $t=2.704$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (e) $x'=-12\cdot\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9\right)$ [M1]; speed $=12.937$ cm/s [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A phase shift is written inside the bracket; set $\dfrac{2\pi}{1.6}t+0.9$ equal to $2\pi$ for the first maximum, and differentiate with the chain rule for speeds.

subtopic: Sine and cosine rule with exact values
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=6$ cm, angle $A=45^\circ$ and angle $B=60^\circ$. (a) Find angle $C$. [1] (b) Use the sine rule to show that $BC=\dfrac{6\sin45^\circ}{\sin75^\circ}$, and find the exact value of $BC$ given that $\sin75^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of triangle $ABC$ using $\dfrac12\,AB\cdot BC\sin B$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $C=180-45-60=75^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{BC}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{6}{\sin75^\circ}$ [M1][A1]; $BC=\dfrac{6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}}=\dfrac{12\sqrt2}{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}=\dfrac{12\sqrt2(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)}{4}=3\sqrt{12}-3\cdot2=6\sqrt3-6$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Area $=\dfrac12(6)(6\sqrt3-6)\sin60^\circ$ [M1]; $=3(6\sqrt3-6)\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1]; $=27-9\sqrt3$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When angles such as $75^\circ$ appear, the question will supply the sine value; rationalize denominators at the end.

subtopic: Cosine rule to find an obtuse angle
statement: Triangle $PQR$ has sides $PQ=3$ cm, $QR=5$ cm and $PR=7$ cm. (a) Use the cosine rule to find the exact value of $\cos\angle PQR$, and hence the size of the angle $PQR$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of triangle $PQR$. [2] (c) Find the exact length of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $QR$ (the height of the triangle with base $QR$). [2]
tips: The largest angle is opposite the longest side; a cosine of $-\tfrac12$ corresponds to $120^\circ$.

subtopic: Bearings and a right-angled triangle with exact values
statement: A hiker walks $4$ km from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $090^\circ$, then $4\sqrt3$ km from $B$ to $C$ on a bearing of $000^\circ$. (a) Find the exact distance $AC$. [2] (b) Find the bearing of $C$ from $A$. [3] (c) Find the bearing of $A$ from $C$. [1] (d) The hiker walks directly from $C$ back to $A$ at $4$ km/h. Find the time taken. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=4^2+(4\sqrt3)^2=16+48=64$ [M1] so $AC=8$ km [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\tan\angle CAB=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{4}=\sqrt3$ [M1] so the angle between $AC$ and east is $60^\circ$ [A1]; bearing $=090^\circ-60^\circ=030^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $030^\circ+180^\circ=210^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac84=2$ hours [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A bearing is measured clockwise from north; the bearing of $A$ from $C$ is the back-bearing, differing by $180^\circ$.

subtopic: Area of a triangle and the cosine rule with unknown angle
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=8$, $AC=5$ and angle $A=60^\circ$. (a) Find the exact length of $BC$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\sin B$, and explain why angle $B$ must be acute. [3]
markscheme: (a) $BC^2=64+25-2(8)(5)\cos60^\circ$ [M1] $=89-40=49$ [A1]; $BC=7$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12(8)(5)\sin60^\circ$ [M1] $=10\sqrt3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin B}{5}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{7}$ [M1]; $\sin B=\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{14}$ [A1]; $B$ is opposite the shortest side $AC=5$, so it is the smallest angle and therefore acute [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The cosine rule finds the third side when two sides and the included angle are known; the sine rule then gives the remaining angles.

subtopic: Angles of elevation from two points
statement: A vertical tower $TP$ stands on level ground with $T$ the top and $P$ the foot. From a point $A$ on the ground the angle of elevation of $T$ is $30^\circ$. Walking $40$ m directly toward the tower to a point $B$, the angle of elevation of $T$ is $60^\circ$. Let the height of the tower be $h$ m. (a) Show that $PA=h\sqrt3$ and $PB=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$. [2] (b) Write down an equation for $h$ using $AB=40$ and hence find the exact value of $h$. [3] (c) Find the exact distance $PB$. [1] (d) Find the exact distance $TB$ from $B$ to the top of the tower. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\tan30^\circ=\dfrac h{PA}$ so $PA=\dfrac{h}{1/\sqrt3}=h\sqrt3$ [A1]; $\tan60^\circ=\dfrac h{PB}=\sqrt3$ so $PB=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PA-PB=40$: $h\sqrt3-\dfrac h{\sqrt3}=40$ [M1]; $h\left(\dfrac{3-1}{\sqrt3}\right)=40$ [A1]; $h=20\sqrt3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $PB=\dfrac{20\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=20$ m [A1] [1 mark] (d) $TB^2=20^2+(20\sqrt3)^2=400+1200=1600$ [M1] so $TB=40$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw two right-angled triangles sharing the vertical side; the two ground distances differ by the distance walked.

subtopic: Two ships leaving a harbor
statement: Two ships leave port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails at $20$ km/h on a bearing of $060^\circ$; ship $B$ sails at $26$ km/h on a bearing of $140^\circ$. Both keep constant velocity. (a) Find the angle between the two directions of travel. [1] (b) Find the distance between the ships after 3 hours. [3] (c) Find the angle $PAB$ and hence the bearing of $B$ from $A$, to the nearest degree. [4]
markscheme: (a) $140^\circ-60^\circ=80^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $AB^2=60^2+78^2-2(60)(78)\cos80^\circ$ [M1][A1]; $AB=89.8$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\sin PAB}{78}=\dfrac{\sin80^\circ}{89.77}$ [M1]; $PAB=58.8^\circ$ [A1]; bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $240^\circ$ [M1]; bearing of $B$ from $A$ $=181^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Draw the triangle $PAB$; the bearing of $B$ from $A$ needs the back-bearing of $P$ from $A$.

subtopic: The ambiguous case of the sine rule
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $a=9$ cm, $b=12$ cm and angle $A=40^\circ$ (the angle opposite side $a$). (a) Show that there are two possible triangles. [3] (b) Find the possible lengths of the third side $c$. [3] (c) Find the area of each triangle. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\sin B}{12}=\dfrac{\sin40^\circ}{9}$ [M1]; $\sin B=0.8571$ so $B=59.0^\circ$ or $B=121.0^\circ$ [A1]; both give $A+B<180^\circ$ so both triangles exist [R1] [3 marks] (b) $c=\dfrac{9\sin C}{\sin40^\circ}$ [M1]; $C=81.0^\circ$ gives $c=13.83$ [A1]; $C=19.0^\circ$ gives $c=4.56$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12ab\sin C$: $53.34$ and $17.57$ [A1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: The ambiguous case occurs when the given angle is opposite the shorter of the two given sides.

subtopic: Area of a quadrilateral using a diagonal
statement: A field $ABCD$ has $AB=7$ m, $BC=9$ m, $CD=8$ m, $DA=6$ m and the diagonal $AC=10$ m. (a) Find angle $ABC$. [3] (b) Find angle $ADC$. [3] (c) Find the area of the field. [3]
tips: Split the quadrilateral into two triangles along the diagonal; each angle needs the cosine rule.

subtopic: Width of a river by triangulation
statement: To find the width of a river, a surveyor marks two points $A$ and $B$ on one bank, $80$ m apart. A tree $T$ is on the opposite bank. The angles are $\angle TAB=52^\circ$ and $\angle TBA=71^\circ$. (a) Find angle $ATB$. [1] (b) Find the distance $AT$. [3] (c) Find the shortest distance from the tree to the line $AB$, which is the width of the river. [3]
markscheme: (a) $180-52-71=57^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\dfrac{AT}{\sin71^\circ}=\dfrac{80}{\sin57^\circ}$ [M1][A1]; $AT=90.19$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) Width $=AT\sin52^\circ$ [M1][A1]; $=71.07$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance; use the sine of the angle at $A$ in the right-angled triangle.

subtopic: Inverse and composite of linear and quadratic functions
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2 x + 3$ and $g(x)=x^{2} - 1$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (b) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and $(g\circ f)(x)$ in simplified form. [4] (c) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $y=f(x)$ and swap $x$ and $y$ [M1]: $x=2 y + 3$ [A1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(g(x))=2 x^{2} + 1$ [M1][A1]; $g(f(x))=\left(2 x + 3\right)^{2} - 1$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) Set the two expressions equal [M1]: $x=-3 - \frac{\sqrt{22}}{2}$; $x=-3 + \frac{\sqrt{22}}{2}$ [A1][A1] (a repeated root counts once) [3 marks]
tips: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means apply $g$ first, then $f$; the composition is not usually commutative.

subtopic: Composite functions and an equation
statement: Let $f(x)=2 x - 1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$. (a) Find $f^{-1}(x)$. [3] (b) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and $(g\circ f)(x)$ in simplified form. [4] (c) Solve $(f\circ g)(x)=(g\circ f)(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Let $y=f(x)$ and swap $x$ and $y$ [M1]: $x=2 y - 1$ [A1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $f(g(x))=2 x^{2} - 1$ [M1][A1]; $g(f(x))=\left(2 x - 1\right)^{2}$ [M1][A1] [4 marks] (c) Set the two expressions equal [M1]: $x=1$ [A1][A1] (a repeated root counts once) [3 marks]
tips: Swap $x$ and $y$ and solve for $y$ to find an inverse; verify with $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$.

subtopic: Domain, range and asymptotes of a rational function
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$ for $x\neq3$. (a) Write down the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of the graph of $f$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the $x$-and $y$-intercepts. [2] (c) Write down the range of $f$. [1] (d) Find $f^{-1}(x)$, state its domain, and comment on how it relates to part (c). [4]
markscheme: (a) $x=3$ [A1]; $y=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=0$: $x=-\dfrac12$ [A1]; $x=0$: $y=-\dfrac13$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)\in\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)\neq2$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $y(x-3)=2x+1$ [M1]; $x(y-2)=3y+1$ [A1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3x+1}{x-2}$ [A1]; domain $x\neq2$, equal to the range of $f$ [R1] [4 marks]
tips: The range of a function is the domain of its inverse; for $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ the horizontal asymptote is $y=a/c$.

subtopic: Even and odd functions and symmetry
statement: The functions $f(x)=x^3-4x$, $g(x)=x^2-4$ and $h(x)=x^3+x^2$ are defined for all real $x$. (a) Find $f(-x)$ and $g(-x)$. State which of $f$ and $g$ is even and which is odd. [3] (b) Show that $h$ is neither even nor odd. [2] (c) Describe the symmetry of the graph of $f$ and write down its zeros. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=-x^3+4x=-f(x)$ [A1]; $g(-x)=x^2-4=g(x)$ [A1]; $f$ is odd and $g$ is even [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h(-x)=-x^3+x^2$ [M1]; this equals neither $h(x)$ nor $-h(x)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Rotational symmetry of order 2 about the origin [A1]; $x(x^2-4)=0$ [M1] gives $x=-2,0,2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: An even function satisfies $f(-x)=f(x)$ (symmetric in the $y$-axis); an odd function satisfies $f(-x)=-f(x)$ (symmetric about the origin).

subtopic: Domain of a composite with a square root
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=\sqrt{x-2}$ for $x\geq2$ and $g(x)=x^2+1$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the range of $f$ and the range of $g$. [2] (b) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Explain why $(g\circ f)(x)$ has a different domain from $(f\circ g)(x)$ and find the domain of $g\circ f$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Range of $f$: $f(x)\geq0$ [A1]; range of $g$: $g(x)\geq1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(g(x))=\sqrt{x^2+1-2}=\sqrt{x^2-1}$ [M1][A1]; domain $|x|\geq1$, i.e. $x\leq-1$ or $x\geq1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $g\circ f$ requires $x$ in the domain of $f$ first [R1]: $x\geq2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The domain of $f\circ g$ is the set of $x$ in the domain of $g$ whose value $g(x)$ lies in the domain of $f$.

subtopic: Range of a cubic on a closed interval
statement: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$ for $0\leq x\leq5$. (a) Use your calculator to find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum points. [3] (b) Hence find the range of $f$. [3] (c) Explain why $f$ has no inverse function on this domain. [1] (d) Find the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=3$. [3] (e) State a largest interval containing $x=4$ on which $f$ has an inverse. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=0$ [M1]; local maximum $(1,5)$ [A1]; local minimum $(3,1)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Compare turning points with the endpoints $f(0)=1$ and $f(5)=21$ [M1][A1]; range $1\leq f(x)\leq21$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $f$ is not one-to-one (it fails the horizontal line test, e.g. $f(0)=f(3)=1$) [R1] [1 mark] (d) Solve on the GDC [M1]: $x=0.268$, $x=2$, $x=3.732$ [A2] (award A1 for two correct) [3 marks] (e) $3\leq x\leq5$ (where $f$ is increasing) [A1] [1 mark]
tips: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one; restrict the domain to an interval on which it is monotonic.

subtopic: Exponential function and its inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=1.5e^{0.4x}-2$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the range of $f$ and the equation of the horizontal asymptote. [2] (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Find $f^{-1}(10)$. [1] (d) Solve $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ using your calculator. [3] (e) Explain why any solution of $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ lies on the line $y=x$ if $f$ is increasing. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)>-2$ [A1]; $y=-2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=1.5e^{0.4x}-2$, swap: $x+2=1.5e^{0.4y}$ [M1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{1}{0.4}\ln\left(\dfrac{x+2}{1.5}\right)=2.5\ln\left(\dfrac{x+2}{1.5}\right)$ [A1]; domain $x>-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $5.199$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) Intersection of $y=f(x)$ and $y=f^{-1}(x)$ [M1]: $x=-0.991$, $x=3.020$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (e) The graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are reflections in $y=x$, and for an increasing function they can only meet on that line [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Swapping $x$ and $y$ reflects the graph in $y=x$; the range of $f$ becomes the domain of the inverse.

subtopic: A rational function and a line
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{3x-2}{x+1}$ for $x\neq-1$, and $g(x)=0.5x-0.5$. (a) Write down the equations of the asymptotes of $y=f(x)$. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the intercepts of the graph of $f$ with the axes. [2] (c) Use your calculator to solve $f(x)=g(x)$. [3] (d) Hence solve $f(x)>g(x)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $x=-1$ [A1]; $y=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x$-intercept $\left(\dfrac23,0\right)$ [A1]; $y$-intercept $(0,-2)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Intersections [M1]: $x=0.551$ and $x=5.449$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Test a value in each interval created by the asymptote $x=-1$ and the intersections [M1]; $f>g$ for $x<-1$ [A1] and for $0.551<x<5.449$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Always consider the asymptote when solving inequalities: $f$ is not defined at $x=-1$, and the sign of $f(x)-g(x)$ can change there.

subtopic: Solving an equation with a modulus function
statement: Let $f(x)=|x^2-4x|$. (a) Sketch (or describe) the graph of $f$ and write down its range. [2] (b) Find the zeros of $f$ and the coordinates of the local maximum of $f$ for $0<x<4$. [3] (c) Use your calculator to solve $f(x)=3$. [3] (d) Hence solve $f(x)\leq3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Graph of $x^2-4x$ with the part below the $x$-axis reflected upward [A1]; range $f(x)\geq0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x(x-4)=0$: $x=0,4$ [A1]; on $0<x<4$, $f=4x-x^2$ with maximum at $x=2$ [M1]; $(2,4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Intersections of $y=f(x)$ and $y=3$ [M1]: $x=-0.646$, $x=1.000$, $x=3.000$, $x=4.646$ [A2] [3 marks] (d) Between consecutive solutions where the graph lies below $y=3$ [M1]: $-0.646\leq x\leq1.000$ and $3.000\leq x\leq4.646$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The modulus reflects the negative part of the graph in the $x$-axis; the equation $|g|=k$ can have up to four solutions for a quadratic $g$.

subtopic: Composite function with a logarithm
statement: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x+1$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and $g(x)=\ln x+x$ for $x>0$. (a) State the largest possible domain of $g\circ f$. [2] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(2)$. [2] (c) Solve $(g\circ f)(x)=4$. [2] (d) Show that $g$ is increasing for $x>0$, and explain why $g$ has an inverse. [3] (e) Find $g^{-1}(4)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f(x)>0$ required [M1]: $x>-\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $g(5)=\ln5+5=6.609$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) Solve $\ln(2x+1)+2x+1=4$ [M1]: $x=0.963$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $g'(x)=\dfrac1x+1>0$ for $x>0$ [M1][A1]; strictly increasing so one-to-one, hence an inverse exists [R1] [3 marks] (e) Solve $g(x)=4$: $x=2.926$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The domain of a composite is limited by the inner function's range falling inside the outer function's domain.

subtopic: Number of solutions of a quadratic depending on a parameter
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-6x+k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $f$ in terms of $k$. [2] (b) Find the values of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=0$ has two distinct real solutions. [3] (c) Given $k=5$, use your calculator to find the zeros of $f$ and the range of $f$. [3] (d) For $k=5$, find the largest domain of the form $x\geq a$ on which $f$ has an inverse, and find $f^{-1}(x)$ for this domain. [4]
markscheme: (a) $x=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$ [A1]; $f(3)=k-9$, vertex $(3,k-9)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\Delta=36-4k>0$ [M1][A1]; $k<9$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Zeros $x=1$ and $x=5$ [A1][A1]; range $f(x)\geq-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $a=3$ [A1]; $y=(x-3)^2-4$, swap and solve [M1]: $x+4=(y-3)^2$ so $f^{-1}(x)=3+\sqrt{x+4}$ [A1][A1] (positive root because $x\geq3$) [4 marks]
tips: The discriminant decides the number of real roots; to invert a quadratic, restrict the domain to one side of the vertex.

subtopic: A piecewise postage function and its inverse
statement: This question investigates a postage function. The cost $C(w)$ dollars of sending a parcel of mass $w$ kg is: $C=6$ for $0<w\leq2$; $C=6+1.5(w-2)$ for $2<w\leq10$; $C=18+1.1(w-10)$ for $10<w\leq30$. (a) Find $C(1)$, $C(2)$, $C(6)$ and $C(10)$. [3] (b) Show that the function is continuous at $w=10$, and state the range of $C$. [3] (c) Explain why $C$ does not have an inverse on $0<w\leq30$, and state the largest domain of the form $2<w\leq b$ on which it does. [3] (d) Find the inverse function $C^{-1}(c)$ for each piece and state its domain. [5] (e) A customer has \$25 to send a parcel. Find the greatest mass that can be sent, to 3 significant figures. [2] (f) The company introduces a discount of $10\%$ on all parcels, $D(w)=0.9C(w)$. Describe the effect on the graph of $C$ and find the greatest mass that can be sent for \$25 now. [4] (g) Find the average cost per kilogram for a $30$ kg parcel and compare it with that for a $4$ kg parcel. Comment. [2]
markscheme: (a) $C(1)=6$, $C(2)=6$ [A1]; $C(6)=6+1.5(4)=12$ [A1]; $C(10)=6+1.5(8)=18$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $6+1.5(8)=18=18+1.1(0)$ [M1][A1]; range $6\leq C\leq40$ since $C(30)=18+22=40$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $C$ is constant on $0<w\leq2$ so it is not one-to-one [R1]; strictly increasing for $w>2$, so $2<w\leq30$ [A1][A1] ($b=30$) [3 marks] (d) First piece: $c=6+1.5(w-2)$ gives $w=2+\dfrac{c-6}{1.5}$ for $6<c\leq18$ [M1][A1]; second piece: $c=18+1.1(w-10)$ gives $w=10+\dfrac{c-18}{1.1}$ for $18<c\leq40$ [M1][A1][A1] [5 marks] (e) $25>18$ so use the second piece [M1]: $w=10+\dfrac{7}{1.1}=16.36\approx16.4$ kg [A1] [2 marks] (f) Vertical stretch with scale factor $0.9$ [A1]; $0.9C=25$ gives $C=27.778$ [M1]; $w=10+\dfrac{27.778-18}{1.1}$ [A1]; $w=18.89$ kg [A1] [4 marks] (g) $\dfrac{40}{30}=1.33$ per kg and $\dfrac{9.0}{4}=2.25$ per kg [A1]; heavier parcels are cheaper per kilogram because of the lower rate of the last piece [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A piecewise function is invertible only if it is strictly monotonic; find each piece's inverse on the image of that piece.

subtopic: Image points under a stretch and translation
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the points $(0,1)$, $(2,-1)$, $(4,3)$. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a vertical stretch of scale factor $2$, a translation $1$ unit to the right and $3$ units up. Hence $g(x)=2f(x-1)+3$. (a) Write down the coordinates of the images of the given points on the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (b) Given that $f$ has a maximum value of $3$ at $x=4$, write down the maximum value of $g$ and where it occurs. [2]
markscheme: (a) Apply the transformations in the correct order [M1]: $(0,1)\to(1,5)$, $(2,-1)\to(3,1)$, $(4,3)\to(5,9)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) Maximum of $g$: $2(3)+3=9$ [A1] at $x=5$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Horizontal translation changes $x$ only; vertical stretch and translation change $y$ only, stretch first then translate.

subtopic: Reflection in the x-axis and a translation
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$ passes through the points $(1,2)$, $(3,0)$, $(5,-4)$. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a translation $2$ units left, a reflection in the $x$-axis and a translation $1$ unit up. Hence $g(x)=-f(x+2)+1$. (a) Write down the coordinates of the images of the given points on the graph of $y=g(x)$. [3] (b) Given that $f$ has a zero at $x=3$, find the zero(s) of $g(x)$ in terms of this, or explain why a zero cannot be found directly. [2]
markscheme: (a) Apply the transformations in the correct order [M1]: $(1,2)\to(-1,-1)$, $(3,0)\to(1,1)$, $(5,-4)\to(3,5)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $g(x)=0$ needs $f(x+2)=1$ [A1]; the zero of $f$ at $x=3$ does not give a zero of $g$ directly, since $g$ is also shifted vertically [R1] [2 marks]
tips: a translation $2$ units left, a reflection in the $x$-axis, and a translation $1$ unit up

subtopic: Transformations of a quadratic graph
statement: The graph of $y=x^2$ is transformed by a translation $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$, followed by a vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ about the $x$-axis, followed by a reflection in the $x$-axis. (a) Find the equation of the resulting graph in the form $y=a(x-h)^2+k$. [4] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and state whether it is a maximum or minimum. [2] (c) Find the $x$-intercepts of the resulting graph, in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) Translation: $y=(x-3)^2-2$ [M1][A1]; stretch: $y=2(x-3)^2-4$ [A1]; reflection: $y=-2(x-3)^2+4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) Vertex $(3,4)$ [A1]; maximum, since the parabola opens downward [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-2(x-3)^2+4=0$ [M1]; $(x-3)^2=2$ [A1]; $x=3\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Apply the transformations in the order stated; a vertical stretch multiplies the whole expression (including constants) by the scale factor.

subtopic: Transformations of an exponential graph
statement: The graph of $y=e^x$ is transformed by a horizontal stretch of scale factor $\dfrac12$, then a translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$, then a reflection in the $y$-axis. (a) Find the equation of the final graph. [3] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and the $y$-intercept. [2] (c) Find the exact $x$-intercept. [2]
markscheme: (a) Horizontal stretch: $y=e^{2x}$ [A1]; translation: $y=e^{2x}-4$ [A1]; reflection: $y=e^{-2x}-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=-4$ [A1]; $(0,-3)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $e^{-2x}=4$ [M1]; $x=-\dfrac12\ln4=-\ln2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch of scale factor $k$ replaces $x$ by $x/k$.

subtopic: Finding the parameters of a transformation from points
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x$. The graph of $g(x)=af(x-b)+c$ is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a vertical stretch, a horizontal translation and a vertical translation. The graph of $g$ passes through $(0,7)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,-1)$ and $b=1$. (a) Write $g(0)$, $g(1)$ and $g(2)$ in terms of $a$ and $c$. [3] (b) Hence find $a$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum of the graph of $g$. [3] (d) Use your calculator to solve $g(x)=10$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(0)=af(-1)+c=2a+c$ [A1]; $g(1)=af(0)+c=c$ [A1]; $g(2)=af(1)+c=-2a+c$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) From $g(1)=c$: $c=3$ [A1]; $2a+3=7$ so $a=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f$ has a local maximum $(-1,2)$ and a local minimum $(1,-2)$ [A1]; image points: $(0,2(2)+3)=(0,7)$ and $(2,2(-2)+3)=(2,-1)$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) Solve on the GDC [M1]: $x=3.151$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute the given points into $g(x)=af(x-b)+c$ using the known values of $f$; the turning points of $f$ move with the same transformation.

subtopic: Graphs of |f(x)| and f(|x|)
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$. Consider the graphs of $y=|f(x)|$ and $y=f(|x|)$. (a) Find the zeros of $f$ and the vertex of $y=f(x)$. [3] (b) Describe how the graph of $y=|f(x)|$ is obtained from that of $y=f(x)$, and write down its range and the greatest value of $|f(x)|$ on $-2\leq x\leq4$. [3] (c) Use your calculator to solve $|f(x)|=2$. [3] (d) Describe the graph of $y=f(|x|)$ and use your calculator to solve $f(|x|)=2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(x-3)(x+1)=0$ so $x=-1,3$ [A1][A1]; vertex $(1,-4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) Reflect the part below the $x$-axis in the $x$-axis [A1]; range $y\geq0$ [A1]; greatest value on the interval is $5$ (at $x=-2$ and $x=4$) [A1] [3 marks] (c) Intersections [M1]: $x=-1.449$, $x=-0.414$, $x=2.414$, $x=3.449$ [A2] [3 marks] (d) Reflect the part with $x\geq0$ in the $y$-axis (symmetric in the $y$-axis) [A1]; solutions $x=-3.449$, $x=3.449$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: $|f(x)|$ reflects negative $y$-values upward; $f(|x|)$ copies the right half of the graph onto the left.

subtopic: Seasonal shift of a sinusoidal model
statement: In a city the mean daily temperature $T^\circ$C in year 1 is modeled by $T_1(m)=12+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(m-4)\right)$, where $m$ is the month number. In year 2 the model is $T_2(m)=14+8\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(m-3.5)\right)$. (a) Describe the transformations that map the graph of $T_1$ onto the graph of $T_2$. [2] (b) State the greatest and least values predicted by $T_2$, and the month number of the greatest value. [3] (c) Use your calculator to find the values of $m$ in $1\leq m\leq12$ for which $T_2(m)=T_1(m)$. [3] (d) Find the difference $T_2(m)-T_1(m)$ on average over a year and explain. [2]
markscheme: (a) Translation $0.5$ units left [A1] and $2$ units up [A1] [2 marks] (b) $14+8=22$ and $14-8=6$ [A1][A1]; $\dfrac\pi6(m-3.5)=\dfrac\pi2$ gives $m=6.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Intersections [M1]: $m=9.192$, $m=10.308$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (d) The sinusoidal parts have the same shape so the average of each over a year is its midline [M1]: difference of midlines $=14-12=2^\circ$C [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A transformation of a sinusoid changes its midline (vertical shift) and its phase (horizontal shift); averages over a full period equal the midline.

subtopic: Effect of stretches on turning points
statement: Let $f(x)=xe^{-x/3}$ for $x\geq0$ and let $g(x)=2f\left(\dfrac x2\right)$. (a) Use your calculator to find the maximum point of $f$. [2] (b) Describe the transformations from $y=f(x)$ to $y=g(x)$. [2] (c) Write down the maximum point of $g$. [2] (d) Find the zero(s) of $g$ and the equation of the horizontal asymptote. [2] (e) Solve $g(x)=1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) Maximum at $x=3.00$, $y=1.104$ [A1][A1] (exact: $(3,3e^{-1})$) [2 marks] (b) Horizontal stretch scale factor $2$ [A1]; vertical stretch scale factor $2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(2\times3.00,2\times1.104)=(6.00,2.207)$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (d) $g(0)=0$, the only zero [A1]; $y=0$ as $x\to\infty$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) Solve on the GDC [M1]: $x=1.227$, $x=16.999$ [A1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch of scale factor $a$ multiplies $x$-coordinates by $a$; a vertical stretch of scale factor $b$ multiplies $y$-coordinates by $b$.

subtopic: Reflections of a logarithmic graph
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln(x+3)$ for $x>-3$. The graph of $g$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the $y$-axis, and the graph of $h$ is the reflection of $f$ in the $x$-axis. (a) Write down expressions for $g(x)$ and $h(x)$, and state the domain of $g$. [3] (b) Find the equations of the vertical asymptotes of $g$ and of $h$. [2] (c) Find the $x$-intercepts of $f$, $g$ and $h$. [3] (d) Use your calculator to find the points where $y=g(x)$ meets the line $y=0.5x-0.2$. [3]
tips: Reflection in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $-x$ (the domain reverses); reflection in the $x$-axis negates the function.

subtopic: Space diagonal and angle in a cuboid (exact)
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has base $ABCD$ with $AB=6$ cm and $BC=8$ cm, and height $AE=5\sqrt3$ cm, where $E$ is above $A$. (a) Find the exact length of the diagonal $AC$ of the base. [2] (b) Find the exact length of the space diagonal $AG$. [2] (c) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$, giving the exact value of its tangent. [3] (d) Find the exact volume and total surface area of the cuboid. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC^2=36+64=100$ [M1] so $AC=10$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AG^2=AC^2+CG^2=100+75=175$ [M1]; $AG=5\sqrt7$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) The angle is $\angle GAC$ [R1]; $\tan\angle GAC=\dfrac{CG}{AC}=\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{10}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $V=6\times8\times5\sqrt3=240\sqrt3$ [A1]; $S=2(48+30\sqrt3+40\sqrt3)$ [M1]; $=96+140\sqrt3$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane.

subtopic: Square-based pyramid with exact lengths
statement: $VABCD$ is a right pyramid with a square base $ABCD$ of side $8$ cm and vertex $V$ vertically above the centre $O$ of the base. The height $VO$ is $6$ cm. (a) Find the exact length of $AC$ and hence the length $AO$. [2] (b) Find the exact length of the sloping edge $VA$. [2] (c) Find the exact height $VM$ of a triangular face, where $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. [2] (d) Find the exact total surface area and the volume. [4]
tips: Right-angled triangles inside the pyramid (using the height, half the base diagonal and half the side) give every length.

subtopic: Cone and hemisphere composite (exact)
statement: A solid is made from a cone of radius $3$ cm and height $4$ cm, joined at its circular base to a hemisphere of radius $3$ cm. (a) Find the slant height of the cone. [1] (b) Find the exact volume of the solid. [3] (c) Find the exact total surface area of the solid (curved surfaces only, since the base is joined). [3]
markscheme: (a) $l=\sqrt{9+16}=5$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (b) Cone: $\dfrac13\pi(9)(4)=12\pi$ [A1]; hemisphere: $\dfrac23\pi(27)=18\pi$ [A1]; total $30\pi$ cm$^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Cone curved: $\pi rl=15\pi$ [A1]; hemisphere curved: $2\pi r^2=18\pi$ [A1]; total $33\pi$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: When two solids are joined, the joining face is not part of the surface area.

subtopic: Sector of a circle folded into a cone
statement: A sector of a circle of radius $10$ cm and angle $\dfrac{6\pi}{5}$ radians is formed into a cone by joining its two straight edges. (a) Find the arc length of the sector. [2] (b) Show that the base radius of the cone is $6$ cm. [2] (c) Find the exact height of the cone. [2] (d) Find the exact volume of the cone. [2]
markscheme: (a) $s=10\times\dfrac{6\pi}{5}$ [M1] $=12\pi$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Arc length is the base circumference: $2\pi r=12\pi$ [M1] so $r=6$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) Slant height $10$: $h^2=100-36=64$ [M1] so $h=8$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\dfrac13\pi(36)(8)$ [M1] $=96\pi$ cm$^3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The slant height of the cone is the radius of the sector, and the arc length becomes the circumference of the base.

subtopic: Triangular prism with an angle between planes
statement: A triangular prism has a horizontal rectangular base $ABCD$ with $AB=12$ cm and $BC=5$ cm, and a ridge $EF$ parallel to $AB$ directly above the midline of the base so that the cross-section is an isosceles triangle of base $5$ cm and height $6$ cm. (a) Find the exact slant height of each sloping face (the equal sides of the triangle). [2] (b) Find the volume of the prism. [2] (c) Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between a sloping face and the base. [2] (d) Find the total surface area of the prism (including both ends and the base). [3]
markscheme: (a) Half the base is $2.5$; slant $=\sqrt{2.5^2+6^2}=\sqrt{42.25}$ [M1]; $=6.5$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) Cross-section area $=\dfrac12(5)(6)=15$ [A1]; $V=15\times12=180$ cm$^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{6}{2.5}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{12}{5}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) Two sloping rectangles: $2(12)(6.5)=156$ [A1]; two triangular ends: $2(15)=30$ [A1]; base $12\times5=60$; total $246$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The angle between two planes is measured perpendicular to their line of intersection.

subtopic: Rectangular-based pyramid: edges and faces
statement: $VABCD$ is a right pyramid with a rectangular base $ABCD$, $AB=12$ cm and $BC=8$ cm. The vertex $V$ is $9$ cm vertically above the centre $O$ of the base. (a) Find the length of the sloping edge $VA$. [3] (b) Find the angle between $VA$ and the base. [2] (c) Find the angle between the face $VAB$ and the base, and between the face $VBC$ and the base. [4] (d) Find the total surface area of the pyramid. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{144+64}=14.422$ [A1]; $AO=7.211$ [A1]; $VA=\sqrt{9^2+7.211^2}=11.53$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{9}{7.211}$ [M1]; $\theta=51.3^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) Face $VAB$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{9}{4}$ (the perpendicular distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $\dfrac{8}{2}=4$) [M1]; $\alpha=66.0^\circ$ [A1]; face $VBC$: $\tan\beta=\dfrac{9}{6}$ [M1]; $\beta=56.3^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) Slant heights $9.849$ and $10.817$ [A1]; area $=96+2\left(\dfrac12\times12\times9.849\right)+2\left(\dfrac12\times8\times10.817\right)$ [M1]; $=300.7$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For the angle between a sloping face and the base, use the perpendicular distance from $O$ to the relevant base edge.

subtopic: Water in a conical tank
statement: A tank is an inverted cone (vertex downward) of radius $6$ m and height $12$ m. It is filled with water to a depth $d$ m. (a) Show that the radius of the water surface is $\dfrac d2$ m. [2] (b) Show that the volume of water is $V=\dfrac{\pi d^3}{12}$. [2] (c) Find the volume of the full tank. [1] (d) Find the depth of the water when the tank is half full. [3] (e) Find the depth at which the volume is $20$ m$^3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) Similar triangles: $\dfrac{r}{d}=\dfrac{6}{12}$ [M1] so $r=\dfrac d2$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2d=\dfrac13\pi\dfrac{d^2}{4}d$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\pi d^3}{12}$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\pi\times12^3}{12}=144\pi=452.4$ m$^3$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{\pi d^3}{12}=72\pi$ [M1]; $d^3=864$ [A1]; $d=9.524$ m [A1] [3 marks] (e) $d=\left(\dfrac{12\times20}{\pi}\right)^{1/3}=4.243$ m [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: Similar triangles link the radius of the water surface to the depth; half the volume is not half the depth.

subtopic: A spherical ball in a cylinder
statement: A sphere of radius $r$ exactly fits inside a closed cylinder (touching the curved surface and both circular ends), with $r=7$ cm. (a) Find the volume of the sphere and the volume of the cylinder. [3] (b) Find the fraction of the cylinder's volume filled by the sphere. [1] (c) Compare the curved surface area of the cylinder with the surface area of the sphere. [3] (d) A solid sphere of radius $7$ cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius $0.5$ cm. Find the number of small spheres. [2]
markscheme: (a) Sphere $=\dfrac43\pi(343)=1436.8$ cm$^3$ [A1]; cylinder $=\pi(49)(14)=2155.1$ cm$^3$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\frac43\pi r^3}{2\pi r^3}=\dfrac23$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) Cylinder curved: $2\pi r(2r)=4\pi r^2=615.8$ [A1]; sphere: $4\pi r^2=615.8$ [A1]; they are equal [R1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{7^3}{0.5^3}$ [M1] $=2744$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A sphere inscribed in a cylinder occupies two thirds of its volume, and their surface areas (curved) are equal.

subtopic: Angles between diagonals of a cuboid
statement: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has $AB=9$ cm, $BC=6$ cm and $CG=7$ cm, with $ABCD$ the horizontal base. $AG$ and $BH$ are two space diagonals. (a) Find the length $AG$. [2] (b) Find the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$. [3] (c) The diagonals $AG$ and $BH$ meet at the centre $M$ of the cuboid. Use the cosine rule in triangle $AMB$ to find angle $AMB$. [4] (d) Hence state the acute angle between the diagonals $AG$ and $BH$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $AG^2=81+36+49=166$ [M1]; $AG=12.88$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $AC=\sqrt{81+36}=10.817$ [A1]; $\tan\theta=\dfrac{7}{10.817}$ [M1]; $\theta=32.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $AM=BM=6.442$ [A1]; $AB=9$; $\cos\angle AMB=\dfrac{2(6.442)^2-81}{2(6.442)^2}$ [M1][A1]; $\angle AMB=88.6^\circ$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $\angle AMB$ is acute; the acute angle between the lines is $88.6^\circ$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Space diagonals of a cuboid all pass through its centre and have equal lengths, giving isosceles triangles.

subtopic: Volume of a frustum by subtracting cones
statement: A bucket has the shape of a frustum of a cone: the top circle has radius $10$ cm, the bottom circle has radius $4$ cm, and the vertical height is $9$ cm. (a) Find the height of the complete cone from which the frustum is cut. [3] (b) Find the volume of the bucket by subtracting a small cone from the large cone. [3] (c) Find how many liters the bucket holds (1 liter $=1000$ cm$^3$). [1] (d) Find the slant height of the frustum and the area of its curved surface. [3]
markscheme: (a) Similar triangles: $\dfrac{H-9}{H}=\dfrac{4}{10}$ [M1][A1]; $H=15$ cm [A1] [3 marks] (b) Large cone $\dfrac13\pi(100)(15)=1570.8$ [A1]; small cone $\dfrac13\pi(16)(6)=100.5$ [A1]; frustum $=1470.3$ cm$^3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $1.47$ liters [A1] [1 mark] (d) Slant $=\sqrt{9^2+6^2}=10.817$ cm [A1]; curved area $=\pi(R+r)\ell=\pi(14)(10.817)$ [M1] $=475.7$ cm$^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A frustum is a large cone minus a small similar cone; the ratio of heights equals the ratio of radii.

subtopic: A wedge-shaped ramp
statement: A ramp is a right triangular prism. Its horizontal base is a rectangle $3.5$ m by $1.2$ m, its vertical back face is a rectangle $0.6$ m by $1.2$ m and the sloping face joins the front edge of the base to the top edge of the back face. (The slope rises $0.6$ m over $3.5$ m of horizontal distance.) (a) Find the angle that the sloping face makes with the horizontal. [2] (b) Find the length of the sloping face and its area. [3] (c) Find the volume of concrete needed to make the ramp. [2] (d) Concrete costs \$145 per cubic meter. Find the cost of the concrete, to the nearest dollar. [2]
tips: The volume of a prism is cross-section area times length; here the cross-section is a right triangle.

subtopic: A flagpole supported by a wire
statement: A vertical flagpole $PQ$ of height $12$ m stands on horizontal ground at $P$. A wire from the top $Q$ is attached to the ground at $R$, where $PR=9$ m. A second wire from $Q$ is attached to the ground at $S$, where $PS=16$ m and angle $RPS=70^\circ$. (a) Find the length of the first wire $QR$ and the angle it makes with the ground. [3] (b) Find the length of $RS$ on the ground. [3] (c) Find the length of the second wire $QS$ and the angle $RQS$ between the wires. [4]
tips: Triangle $QRS$ is not right-angled: find its three sides first, then apply the cosine rule.

subtopic: Standard form arithmetic without a calculator
statement: Let $a=3.6\times10^{5}$ and $b=1.2\times10^{-3}$. (a) Find $\dfrac ab$, giving your answer in the form $k\times10^n$ with $1\leq k<10$. [3] (b) Find $ab$ in the form $k\times10^n$ with $1\leq k<10$. [3] (c) Find $a+b$ correct to 3 significant figures, in the form $k\times10^n$. [2]
tips: When dividing, subtract the exponents; adding numbers of very different sizes leaves the larger one almost unchanged.

subtopic: Percentage error from rounding
statement: The length of a rectangular field is measured as $52$ m and its width as $38$ m. Both measurements are correct to the nearest meter. The exact values are $L=51.6$ m and $W=38.4$ m. (a) Find the percentage error in the measured length. [2] (b) Calculate the area using the measured values, and the area using the exact values. [3] (c) Find the percentage error in the area, correct to 2 significant figures. [2]
tips: Percentage error is $\dfrac{|v_A-v_E|}{|v_E|}\times100$ where $v_E$ is the exact value.

subtopic: Laws of logarithms and exponential equations
statement: Let $\log_2 x=a$ and $\log_2 y=b$. (a) Write $\log_2\left(\dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt y}\right)$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Given that $x=8$ and $y=16$, find $a$, $b$ and the value of the expression in part (a). [3] (c) Solve $2^{x+1}=5$, giving the exact answer in terms of $\log_2 5$ and as a decimal to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: $\log(AB)=\log A+\log B$, $\log A^n=n\log A$; convert exponential equations with $a^x=b\Leftrightarrow x=\log_a b$.

subtopic: Laws of exponents and simplification
statement: Simplify each expression, giving answers in the form $2^p3^q$ or as an integer. (a) $\dfrac{12^3}{18^2}$ [3] (b) $\left(\dfrac{8}{27}\right)^{-2/3}$ [3]
tips: Write bases as prime factors, then subtract exponents when dividing; a negative exponent means reciprocal.

subtopic: Time for exponential growth using logarithms
statement: A town's population is $P(t)=20\,000\times1.04^t$ where $t$ is the number of years from now. (a) Write down the population after 2 years, correct to the nearest person (no calculator needed beyond $1.04^2=1.0816$). [2] (b) Find an exact expression for the number of years for the population to double. [3]
tips: To solve $a^t=k$, take logarithms: $t=\ln k/\ln a$.

subtopic: Currency exchange with commission
statement: A bank exchanges currency at a rate of 1 euro $=1.0845$ US dollars (USD), charging a commission of $2.5\%$ on every transaction (deducted from the amount received). (a) Mia exchanges 2500 USD into euros. Find the amount of euros she receives, correct to the nearest cent. [3] (b) She immediately exchanges all her euros back into USD with the same rate and commission. Find how much she has, and her percentage loss. [4] (c) Explain why a customer who converts currency back and forth with the same rate always loses money. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{2500}{1.0845}=2305.21$ [M1][A1]; after commission $\times0.975=2247.58$ euros [A1] [3 marks] (b) $(2247.58)\times1.0845\times0.975$ [M1][A1]; $=\$2376.56$ [A1]; loss $=4.94\%$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) Each conversion multiplies the amount by $0.975$, a factor less than $1$, and the exchange rates cancel [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Apply the commission after the conversion each time, so two transactions lose about $5\%$ in total.

subtopic: Upper and lower bounds for a calculated quantity
statement: The side of a square tile is measured as $24.5$ cm, correct to 3 significant figures. (a) Write down the lower and upper bounds for the side length. [2] (b) Find the lower and upper bounds for the area of the tile. [3] (c) Hence write the area correct to a number of significant figures that is justified by the bounds. [2]
tips: A value given to a stated accuracy lies within half a unit of the last digit; propagate bounds through squares by squaring the bounds.

subtopic: Successive percentage changes
statement: The price of a laptop is \$900. It is reduced by $15\%$ in a sale, and later increased by $12\%$. (a) Find the final price. [2] (b) Find the overall percentage change in the price. [2] (c) The price must be increased by a certain percentage from the sale price to return to \$900. Find this percentage. [3]
tips: Percentage changes multiply: a reduction of $15\%$ is a factor of $0.85$, and they are not reversible by the same percentage.

subtopic: Cartesian operations on complex numbers
statement: Let $z=3+4i$ and $w=1-2i$. (a) Find $zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ (to 3 significant figures, in radians). [3]
markscheme: (a) $zw=(3 + 4 i)(1 - 2 i)$ [M1] $=11 - 2 i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Multiply numerator and denominator by $\bar w=1 + 2 i$ [M1]; denominator $=5$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=-1 + 2 i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$ [A1]; $\arg z=$ angle in the correct quadrant (use the reference angle $\arctan\left|\dfrac{4}{3}\right|$) [M1] $=0.927$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator to realize it; check the quadrant for the argument.

subtopic: Division of complex numbers and polar form
statement: Let $z=-2+6i$ and $w=2+i$. (a) Find $zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [2] (b) Find $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ (to 3 significant figures, in radians). [3]
markscheme: (a) $zw=(-2 + 6 i)(2 + i)$ [M1] $=-10 + 10 i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Multiply numerator and denominator by $\bar w=2 - i$ [M1]; denominator $=5$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=\frac{2}{5} + \frac{14 i}{5}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $|z|=\sqrt{4+36}=2 \sqrt{10}$ [A1]; $\arg z=$ angle in the correct quadrant (use the reference angle $\arctan\left|\dfrac{6}{-2}\right|$) [M1] $=1.893$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For $z$ in the second quadrant the argument is $\pi-\arctan|b/a|$; a calculator's arctan alone may be wrong.

subtopic: Complex roots of a quadratic equation
statement: Consider the equation $z^2-6z+25=0$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Solve the equation. [3] (b) Write the root with positive imaginary part in the form $re^{i\theta}$, giving $\theta$ to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that the sum of the roots is $6$ and the product is $25$, and explain how these relate to the coefficients. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{6\pm\sqrt{36-100}}{2}$ [M1]; $=\dfrac{6\pm8i}{2}$ [A1]; $z=3\pm4i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=5$ [A1]; $\theta=\arctan\dfrac43$ [M1] $=0.927$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Sum $=(3+4i)+(3-4i)=6$ [A1]; product $=9+16=25$ [A1]; for $z^2+bz+c$, sum $=-b$ and product $=c$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Complex roots of a polynomial with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs; their sum and product are real.

subtopic: Multiplying and dividing in modulus-argument form
statement: Let $z=4\left(\cos\dfrac\pi3+i\sin\dfrac\pi3\right)$ and $w=2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi6+i\sin\dfrac\pi6\right)$. (a) Write $zw$ and $\dfrac zw$ in modulus-argument form. [4] (b) Hence write $zw$ and $\dfrac zw$ in the form $a+bi$. [3] (c) Write $z$ in the form $a+bi$ and verify that $|z|^2=z\bar z$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $|zw|=8$, $\arg(zw)=\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi2$ [M1][A1]; $|z/w|=2$, $\arg=\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi6$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (b) $zw=8\left(\cos\dfrac\pi2+i\sin\dfrac\pi2\right)=8i$ [A1]; $\dfrac zw=2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac i2\right)$ [M1] $=\sqrt3+i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $z=4\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}i\right)=2+2\sqrt3i$ [A1]; $z\bar z=4+12=16$ [M1]; $|z|^2=16$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments; dividing divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.

subtopic: A cubic with a complex root
statement: The cubic $p(z)=z^3-5z^2+17z-13$ has $z=1$ as a root. (a) Show that $z=1$ is a root. [1] (b) Factorize $p(z)$ completely over $\mathbb{C}$. [4] (c) Plot the three roots on an Argand diagram (describe their positions) and find the area of the triangle they form. [2]
